Requests without credentials are public: they can read PUBLISHED content, unless the operator sets TESS_PUBLIC_READ=false. Everything else needs Authorization: Bearer <token>. Token Looks like Obtained with User session tess_s1.… login API token tess_t1_… createApiToken (Admin) Bootstrap token operator-defined TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN, only to create the first Owner Invalid, expired or revoked credentials get HTTP 401. A valid credential without the required permission gets a GraphQL error with code FORBIDDEN.

mutation { login(email: "ada@example.com", password: "…") { token # send as: Authorization: Bearer <token> expiresAt user { name role scope } } } Operation setupRequired: Boolean! true until the first user exists (public) me: User the signed-in user (null for API and bootstrap tokens) changePassword(currentPassword, newPassword): Session! returns a new token; every other session is revoked signOutEverywhere: Boolean! revokes all of your sessions, this one included Sessions last TESS_SESSION_TTL (12 h by default); sign in again afterwards. Passwords need at least 12 characters. After 10 failed attempts, an account is locked for 15 minutes.

Owner Admin Contributor Reviewer Member Manage Owners ✔ Manage users, API tokens, content models, plugins, reindex search ✔ ✔ Publish anything, bypass review ✔ ✔ Approve / request changes (workflow types) ✔ ✔ ✔ Create and edit drafts, submit for review, upload media ✔ ✔ ✔ Publish and unpublish types without workflow ✔ ✔ ✔ Delete entries ✔ ✔ never-published only Read drafts and media ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Scope: a Contributor or Reviewer can be limited to a list of content types (scope). An empty list means every type. Admins and Owners always have access to all types.

mutation { createUser(input: { email: "carl@example.com", name: "Carl Example", role: CONTRIBUTOR, scope: ["Post", "Page"], password: "a long initial password" }) { id role scope } } Operation users: [User!]! list users updateUser(id, input: { name, role, scope, disabled, password }) omitted fields are unchanged deleteUser(id) delete Rules: Owners: only Owners can create, modify or delete them, and there is always at least one active Owner. Yourself: nobody can change their own role, or disable or delete their own account. Sign-out: changing a user's role, scope, status or password signs them out everywhere.

For CI, static-site builds, webhooks and back-ends: mutation { createApiToken(name: "Website build", role: MEMBER, expiresInDays: 90) { token # shown once: store it in your secrets manager apiToken { id name role expiresAt } } } A token acts with its role and scope. Admins can't create Owner tokens. List tokens with apiTokens, and revoke them with revokeApiToken(id). For a front-end that only reads drafts (previews), a MEMBER token is enough. :::tip Single sign-on Sign-in with your identity provider (OIDC) is planned for the Enterprise edition. :::

A component is a reusable set of fields: an SEO block, a call-to-action, a hero banner, an address. You define it once and use it in three ways: Use Field Stored as One instance in a content type COMPONENT an object A list of instances COMPONENT with repeatable: true a list of objects A list mixing several components (page builder) DYNAMIC_ZONE with components: [...] a list of objects, each tagged with its component Inside another component COMPONENT in the component nested objects Component data lives inside the entry, so it is versioned with the draft/published stages and works on every database.

Admins manage components on the Components page of the admin UI, or with the API: mutation { link: createComponent(input: {apiId: "Link", fields: [ { name: "label", type: TEXT, required: true, maxLength: 40 } { name: "url", type: TEXT, pattern: "https?://\\S+" } { name: "page", type: RELATION, relationTarget: "Page" } ]}) { apiId } hero: createComponent(input: {apiId: "Hero", description: "Top banner", fields: [ { name: "title", type: TEXT, required: true } { name: "image", type: RELATION, relationTarget: "Asset" } { name: "cta", type: COMPONENT, component: "Link" } ]}) { apiId } } Shared names: API IDs are PascalCase and shared with content types, so a component can't be named like a content type. Allowed fields: components can contain every field type except PASSWORD and DYNAMIC_ZONE. Nesting: components can be nested up to 5 levels deep, and never inside themselves. Editing: updateComponent replaces the definition, and every model using the component changes immediately. Deleting: deleteComponent is refused while a content type or component still uses it. Listing: components and component(apiId) return the definitions.

mutation { createContentType(input: {apiId: "Page", fields: [ { name: "title", type: TEXT, required: true } { name: "links", type: COMPONENT, component: "Link", repeatable: true } { name: "blocks", type: DYNAMIC_ZONE, components: ["Hero", "Link"] } ]}) { apiId } }

A component field returns the component's object type. A dynamic zone returns a union, so select each possible component with an inline fragment: { pages(where: { title: "Home" }) { items { title links { label url } blocks { __typename ... on Hero { title cta { label url page { title } } image { url } } ... on Link { label url } } } } } Relations inside components resolve in the same stage as the entry: a published page shows published related entries.

Component fields take an input object named after the component (LinkInput). GraphQL has no input unions, so each dynamic zone item is an object with exactly one key, the component to use: mutation($data: PageCreateInput!) { createPage(data: $data) { id } } { "data": { "title": "Home", "links": [{ "label": "Docs", "url": "/docs/" }], "blocks": [ { "Hero": { "title": "Welcome", "cta": { "label": "Start", "url": "https://example.com" } } }, { "Link": { "label": "More" } } ] } } Validation: component fields are validated like top-level fields, and errors name the exact path (blocks[0].cta.url does not match the expected format). Relation ids: relation ids inside components are the usual opaque ids. note Filtering and sorting by fields inside components isn't supported yet.

GraphQL errors come back in errors[], with a machine-readable code in extensions.code: { "data": null, "errors": [{ "message": "you cannot edit `Page` entries", "extensions": { "code": "FORBIDDEN" } }] } Code Typical causes FORBIDDEN not signed in for a non-public operation, role or scope not allowed, wrong password at login, account locked BAD_USER_INPUT validation (missing required field, wrong type, unknown field, bad enum value, invalid id), a plugin rejected the write, request changes without a comment NOT_FOUND the entry, user, plugin or content type doesn't exist CONFLICT duplicate content type or email, generated names would collide, deleting a referenced type, workflow transition not allowed in the current status, removing the last Owner ID_EXPIRED the id is older than TESS_ID_TTL: refetch the entry PLUGIN_ERROR a plugin crashed, timed out or returned invalid output INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR storage failure; details are only in the server logs Unknown fields or arguments (for example a content type that doesn't exist yet) are reported by GraphQL validation, without a code.

Status Meaning 200 GraphQL response, including errors in errors[] 401 invalid, expired or revoked credentials: sign in again 503 the server can't reach its storage to check credentials (and /health when the database is down)

POST /media/upload and POST /api/plugins/{name} answer with JSON {"error": "…", "code": "…"} and a matching status: 400 BAD_USER_INPUT, 401 UNAUTHENTICATED, 403 FORBIDDEN, 404 NOT_FOUND, 409 CONFLICT, 422 PLUGIN_ERROR, 500 INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR.

Content types are managed by Admins, in the admin UI or with these mutations: mutation { createContentType(input: { apiId: "Post" # PascalCase: becomes the GraphQL type name pluralApiId: "posts" # optional (defaults to camelCase + "s") description: "Blog posts" workflow: true # require review before publishing fields: [ { name: "title", type: TEXT, required: true } # max 80 characters by default { name: "slug", type: TEXT, pattern: "[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*" } { name: "contact", type: TEXT, pattern: "[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[a-z]{2,}" } # an email field { name: "excerpt", type: TEXT, minLength: 20, maxLength: 300 } { name: "notes", type: TEXT, maxLength: null } # unlimited { name: "body", type: MARKDOWN } { name: "views", type: INT } { name: "rating", type: FLOAT } { name: "featured", type: BOOLEAN } { name: "date", type: DATE } { name: "updated", type: DATETIME } { name: "code", type: UUID } { name: "pin", type: PASSWORD, minLength: 12 } { name: "meta", type: JSON } { name: "status", type: ENUM, enumValues: ["NEWS", "TUTORIAL"] } { name: "author", type: RELATION, relationTarget: "Author" } { name: "tags", type: RELATION, relationTarget: "Tag", many: true } { name: "cover", type: RELATION, relationTarget: "Asset" } { name: "seo", type: COMPONENT, component: "Seo" } { name: "blocks", type: DYNAMIC_ZONE, components: ["Hero", "Quote"] } ] }) { apiId pluralApiId workflow } } Field type GraphQL type Notes TEXT String minLength (default 0), maxLength (default 80; null for unlimited), pattern MARKDOWN String Markdown or MDX source, rendered by your clients; raw HTML is refused INT / FLOAT Int / Float BOOLEAN Boolean DATETIME DateTime RFC 3339, normalized to UTC with milliseconds (2026-01-31T12:00:00.000Z) DATE Date YYYY-MM-DD, no time UUID UUID normalized to lowercase; generated when left empty on create PASSWORD input only minLength (default 8); hashed, never returned JSON JSON any JSON value ENUM <Type><Field>Enum RELATION the target type, or [Target!]! with many COMPONENT the component type, or [Component!]! with repeatable see Components DYNAMIC_ZONE [<Type><Field>Zone!]! (a union) see Components

pattern is a regular expression in Rust regex syntax, and the whole value must match it. Examples: Format pattern Email [^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,} URL https?://\S+ Slug [a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)* Phone \+[1-9][0-9 ]{6,18} Lookarounds and backreferences aren't supported, which guarantees matching in linear time. Patterns are limited to 500 characters.

MARKDOWN fields keep the source as-is; render it in your clients with the Markdown or MDX library of your choice. Allowed (MDX): components, because they start with an uppercase letter (, , ), as well as {…} expressions and fragments (<>). Allowed (Markdown): autolinks such as and . PASSWORD values are hashed with Argon2id when written; the plain text is never stored. The field isn't part of the output type, filters, sorting, search or plugin inputs (plugins only see the hash). To check a candidate, for example for a password-protected page: query($id: ID!) { verifyPassword(contentType: "Page", id: $id, field: "pin", password: "…") # → true / false } verifyPassword reads the PUBLISHED stage by default, and has the same access rules as reading the entry. Password fields are only allowed directly in content types, not inside components. Naming rules: apiId: PascalCase, letters and digits only. Field names: camelCase, letters and digits only, at most 64 characters. API IDs are shared between content types and components. Reserved field names: id, ref, stage, createdAt, updatedAt, publishedAt, workflowStatus, createdBy, updatedBy, history, where and orderBy. Collisions: names that would collide in the generated schema are rejected with CONFLICT. Other mutations: updateContentType(apiId, input) replaces the whole definition. Send every field you want to keep, and workflow too: omitting it turns the workflow off. Renaming isn't supported. Data of removed fields is hidden, then dropped on the next write. deleteContentType(apiId) deletes the type and all its entries. It's refused while other types still have relations to it. contentTypes and contentType(apiId) list the models. Unlike the mutations (Owner/Admin), they are readable by every signed-in user or token (the admin content manager builds its forms from them), not by anonymous clients. The same goes for components and component(apiId). The built-in Asset type (media) cannot be modified.

For a type Post with plural posts: Operation Purpose post(id: ID!, stage: Stage = PUBLISHED): Post one entry posts(where, orderBy, first, skip, stage): PostConnection! a list: { total items } searchPosts(query: String!, first, skip, stage) full-text search, when search is enabled createPost(data: PostCreateInput!) create a draft updatePost(id, data: PostUpdateInput!) partial update of the draft; null clears a field deletePost(id) delete publishPost(id) / unpublishPost(id) copy the draft to PUBLISHED / remove the published version submitPostForReview, approvePost, requestChangesPost only when the workflow is enabled Every entry type also has these system fields: Field id opaque, expiring id (why) ref stable opaque reference, for cache keys stage DRAFT or PUBLISHED, the version you're looking at createdAt, updatedAt, publishedAt timestamps workflowStatus DRAFT, IN_REVIEW, CHANGES_REQUESTED, PUBLISHED createdBy, updatedBy, history editorial metadata; null for anonymous readers Relation fields resolve to the related entries in the same stage: a published post shows its published author. Related entries that are missing or unpublished are skipped.

mutation($data: PostCreateInput!) { createPost(data: $data) { id ref stage workflowStatus } } { "data": { "title": "Hello", "slug": "hello", "author": "<author id>", "tags": ["<tag id>"] } } Relation inputs take entry ids, which must be fresh (they expire). updatePost merges the given fields into the draft; send null to clear a field. Required fields must always be present.
Queries return PUBLISHED content by default. Ask for drafts with stage: DRAFT; that requires being signed in. Publishing copies the current draft to the published version.

When an Admin changes a content model, the instance handling the request rebuilds its schema immediately. Other instances do so within TESS_SCHEMA_REFRESH_SECS, or at once when they share a Valkey cache. A request can't use the operations of a type created in the same request.

Tess never exposes database ids. Every entry has two identifiers instead: id ref Looks like AXuW71Xk… (long) 4_vBlX0sxaaBG_AdKSON2g Stable no: different in every response yes Expires yes, after TESS_ID_TTL (24 h by default) never Accepted as input yes: post(id:), mutations, relations, where: { id… } no Use it for an immediate follow-up call React/Vue keys, caches, deduplication Ids are encrypted and bound to their type. An Author id passed where a Post id is expected is rejected (BAD_USER_INPUT). After expiry they're rejected with ID_EXPIRED: query the entry again to get a fresh id.

Route by your own fields, typically a slug: posts(where: { slug: $slug }, first: 1). Never put an id in a URL. Use ref for list keys and cache keys, and to recognize the same entry across responses. Never store ids in a database, a static build or localStorage. Relations take ids: fetch the related entries, then write right away. Plugins receive ref too, never ids.

Tess includes a Model Context Protocol server, so AI agents (Claude, Cursor, and other MCP clients) can read and write content through the same GraphQL API as your applications. The server exposes two generic tools, so it works with any content model without reconfiguration: Tool Purpose get_schema Returns the GraphQL schema. Pass type (for example Post) to read one type only. Agents call it first to discover content types and operations. graphql_query Runs a query or mutation with optional variables and operationName. Returns the JSON response, with data and errors. Agents can do everything the GraphQL API allows for the credential they use: the rules in Authentication, roles and API tokens apply unchanged.

The endpoint is off by default. Turn it on in the server environment: TESS_MCP=true # Host headers accepted on /mcp. Add your public hostname in production. TESS_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost,127.0.0.1,::1,cms.example.com With TESS_MCP=true, the endpoint is served at https://<your-host>/mcp. It uses the stateless Streamable HTTP transport, so it works on several instances and on AWS Lambda.

Every client authenticates the same way: it sends an API token in the Authorization header of each request to /mcp: Authorization: Bearer tess_t1_… Create one token per agent in the admin (API tokens) or with createApiToken. The token is shown once: copy it into an environment variable (here TESS_MCP_TOKEN), not into a file you might commit. Its role is the agent's role. A Contributor token writes drafts but can't change models; an Admin token can. See Choosing a token for agents. Without the header, the agent is anonymous: it reads published content only, and only if TESS_PUBLIC_READ is enabled. An invalid, expired or revoked token gets a 401, and the client reports the server as failed. Write Bearer, a space, then the token. Most clients read the token from an environment variable (the syntax differs per client, see below), so set it in the shell or service that starts the client: export TESS_MCP_TOKEN=tess_t1_…

There are two ways to connect, with the same tools and access rules: Remote (HTTP): the client calls https://<your-host>/mcp directly and sends the token in the Authorization header. Use it whenever the client supports remote servers with custom headers. Local (stdio): the client starts tess mcp, a small local proxy that forwards each call to your server with the token. Use it for clients that only start local programs. It needs the tess binary on that machine (from the release archives), but no database and none of the server's secrets. Client How Token Claude Code Remote --header "Authorization: Bearer …" or ${TESS_MCP_TOKEN} in .mcp.json Claude Desktop Local (tess mcp) TESS_MCP_TOKEN in env OpenCode Remote "Authorization": "Bearer {env:TESS_MCP_TOKEN}" Codex Remote bearer_token_env_var = "TESS_MCP_TOKEN" Pi Remote "Authorization": "Bearer ${TESS_MCP_TOKEN}" Others Remote or local an Authorization header, or TESS_MCP_TOKEN for tess mcp In the examples, replace https://cms.example.com with your Tess URL.

Add the server with the CLI (--scope user makes it available in every project): claude mcp add --transport http tess https://cms.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${TESS_MCP_TOKEN}" --scope user Or share it with your team in the project's .mcp.json, with the token read from each person's environment (${TESS_MCP_TOKEN} is expanded by Claude Code, so the file holds no secret): { "mcpServers": { "tess": { "type": "http", "url": "https://cms.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${TESS_MCP_TOKEN}" } } } } Check it with /mcp in a session. Use your own variable name: Claude Code doesn't expand its own credential variables (such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) in headers.

Claude Desktop's connectors sign in with OAuth and can't send a fixed Authorization header, so use the local proxy. In Settings → Developer → Edit Config, add Tess to claude_desktop_config.json (~/Library/Application Support/Claude/ on macOS, %APPDATA%\Claude\ on Windows), then restart Claude Desktop: { "mcpServers": { "tess": { "command": "tess", "args": ["mcp"], "env": { "TESS_MCP_URL": "https://cms.example.com", "TESS_MCP_TOKEN": "tess_t1_…" } } } } tess mcp sends TESS_MCP_TOKEN as the Authorization: Bearer header. Use the full path of the binary in command if it isn't on the PATH ("/usr/local/bin/tess", or "C:\\Tess\\tess.exe" on Windows: backslashes are doubled in JSON).

In opencode.json (in the project, or the global OpenCode config), with oauth: false so OpenCode doesn't try to sign in with OAuth: { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "mcp": { "tess": { "type": "remote", "url": "https://cms.example.com/mcp", "enabled": true, "oauth": false, "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:TESS_MCP_TOKEN}" } } } } {env:TESS_MCP_TOKEN} is replaced with the environment variable. Check the connection with opencode mcp debug tess.

In ~/.codex/config.toml (or .codex/config.toml in a trusted project). Codex reads the token from the variable named in bearer_token_env_var and sends it as Authorization: Bearer …: [mcp_servers.tess] url = "https://cms.example.com/mcp" bearer_token_env_var = "TESS_MCP_TOKEN" Start Codex from a shell where TESS_MCP_TOKEN is set, and check with codex mcp list.

Pi supports MCP from version 1.0. Add Tess to ~/.pi/agent/mcp.json (or .pi/mcp.json in a trusted project); ${TESS_MCP_TOKEN} is read from the environment: { "mcpServers": { "tess": { "url": "https://cms.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${TESS_MCP_TOKEN}" }, "description": "Read and edit the website content in Tess" } } } Check it with pi mcp list, or /mcp in a session (/reload after editing the file). With an MCP extension such as pi-mcp-adapter installed, Pi uses the extension's configuration instead: see its documentation.

Any MCP client works. With remote servers and custom headers, use the URL and the Authorization: Bearer header, as above. Otherwise, start the local proxy: command tess, arguments mcp, environment TESS_MCP_URL (default http://localhost:8080) and TESS_MCP_TOKEN.

Create a dedicated API token for each agent, with the lowest role that does the job. Admins create tokens with createApiToken, and an expiry keeps a leaked token short-lived: Agent does Suggested role Reads drafts and published content MEMBER Creates and edits drafts CONTRIBUTOR (limit it with scope) Approves workflow reviews REVIEWER Revoke a token with revokeApiToken if it is no longer needed.

Mutations are allowed, but limited by role. A MEMBER token can read drafts but cannot write. Restrict agents with scope to the content types they should touch. Query limits still apply. Maximum depth (TESS_MAX_QUERY_DEPTH) and page size (TESS_MAX_PAGE_SIZE) are enforced by the GraphQL schema. Size limits. A query is refused above 32 KiB, and a result above 256 KiB. The agent receives an error explaining how to narrow the request. Ids expire. Fetch an entry again before using its id in a mutation (see IDs and refs).

401 on /mcp: the token is invalid, expired or revoked. Check the header reads Bearer, a space, then the token, and that the environment variable is set where the client runs: an unset variable sends Bearer alone, or the variable's name. The client opens a sign-in page or asks for OAuth: Tess uses API tokens, not OAuth. Send the Authorization header (OpenCode: "oauth": false), or use the local tess mcp proxy. Only published content, and "sign in required" on writes: no token reached Tess, so the agent is anonymous. 403 with "Host header is not allowed": add the hostname to TESS_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS. isError: true with FORBIDDEN: the token's role or scope does not allow the operation. cannot reach the GraphQL endpoint (stdio): check TESS_MCP_URL and that the server is running.

Uploaded files are entries of the built-in Asset content type: Field fileName, mimeType, size file metadata key storage key status PENDING (direct upload not confirmed yet) or READY alt, width, height optional, for your front-end url where to download the file To add media to your models, use a relation to Asset ({ name: "cover", type: RELATION, relationTarget: "Asset" }). Uploading requires the Contributor role or above. Deleting an asset deletes its file.

Works with every media store: curl -s -X POST "https://cms.example.com/media/upload?fileName=cat.jpg" \ -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'content-type: image/jpeg' \ --data-binary @cat.jpg The response is the asset as JSON (id, ref, fileName, mimeType, size, url, …), with status 201. Errors use the REST error shape.

With an S3-compatible store, clients can upload straight to the bucket. This is best for large files, and required beyond 6 MB on AWS Lambda. mutation { createAssetUpload(fileName: "video.mp4", mimeType: "video/mp4", size: 52428800) { asset { id status } # PENDING url method expiresIn headers { name value } # send them exactly } } curl -X PUT "$URL" -H "content-type: video/mp4" --data-binary @video.mp4 mutation($id: ID!) { confirmAssetUpload(id: $id) { status size url } } confirmAssetUpload checks that the object exists and is within the size limit, then marks the asset READY. With the filesystem store, createAssetUpload returns BAD_USER_INPUT: use /media/upload.

Asset.url is either a CDN URL, a presigned URL (valid for TESS_MEDIA_URL_TTL_SECS) or a /media/files/… path served by Tess, depending on the server configuration. Presigned URLs expire, so fetch url when you render, don't store it.

Tess exposes one GraphQL endpoint, generated from your content models. Endpoint POST /graphql, with JSON { "query": "…", "variables": { … } } IDE GET /graphql opens GraphiQL, if enabled by the operator Schema GET /graphql/schema.graphql (SDL) Auth Authorization: Bearer <token> (session, API token); none for public reads curl -s https://cms.example.com/graphql \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"query":"{ posts(first: 3) { total items { title } } }"}' const res = await fetch('https://cms.example.com/graphql', { method: 'POST', headers: {'content-type': 'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({query: '{ posts(first: 3) { items { ref title } } }'}), }); const {data, errors} = await res.json();

Model content and use the generated API Filter, sort and paginate Authenticate users and machines Use the review workflow Upload and serve media Search Handle ids and refs correctly Handle errors Start from a client example in Vike, Gatsby, Next.js, Nuxt, Ruby, Python, Lua, PHP, Go or Rust
{ posts( where: { title_contains: "rust", OR: [{ views_gt: 100 }, { featured: true }] } orderBy: [publishedAt_DESC, title_ASC] first: 10 skip: 20 ) { total items { ref title views publishedAt } } }

Filters are named <field>_<operator>. Plain <field> means equality. Field kind Operators TEXT, MARKDOWN field, _not, _in, _not_in, _contains, _not_contains, _starts_with, _ends_with INT, FLOAT, DATETIME, DATE field, _not, _in, _not_in, _lt, _lte, _gt, _gte BOOLEAN field, _not ENUM, UUID, single RELATION (by id) field, _not, _in, _not_in System fields id, createdAt, updatedAt, publishedAt (like DATETIME), workflowStatus (like ENUM) JSON, PASSWORD, many-relations, components and dynamic zones aren't filterable. Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT, which take lists of where inputs (NOT matches when none of its conditions do). Semantics, identical on every database: Missing values behave like null. field: null matches entries without a value, and field_not: null matches entries with one. Comparisons only match values of the same type. String matching (_contains, _starts_with, _ends_with) and string ordering are case-sensitive and bytewise. Date-times in filters may use any RFC 3339 offset; they are normalized to UTC.

A list of <field>_ASC / <field>_DESC values, in priority order. Sortable fields: id, createdAt, updatedAt, publishedAt, and the content fields of type TEXT, MARKDOWN, INT, FLOAT, BOOLEAN, DATETIME, DATE and ENUM. The default order is createdAt_ASC. Ties are always broken by id, so pagination is stable. Missing values sort first in ascending order.

first: page size. It defaults to TESS_DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE (100) and is capped at TESS_MAX_PAGE_SIZE (1000). skip: offset. total: the number of entries matching the filter, regardless of the page. Queries deeper than TESS_MAX_QUERY_DEPTH (16) are rejected.

When the server has a search engine configured (see DevOps: search) and an Admin has enabled search on a content type (Admin → Search), that type gets a search query: { searchPosts(query: "graphql rust", first: 10, skip: 0) { total items { ref title excerpt } } } Ranking: results are ordered by relevance; total is the number of matches. What's searched: the TEXT and MARKDOWN fields the Admin selected. Typo tolerance and ranking come from the engine (Typesense). Drafts: stage: DRAFT searches drafts, which requires being signed in. Published and draft content are indexed separately. Freshness: entries are loaded from the database after the search, so you always get current data. Page size: first defaults to 20 and is capped at 250 (or TESS_MAX_PAGE_SIZE if lower). If searchPosts isn't in the schema, the server has no search engine, or search is not enabled on that type.

Every entry has a draft and, once published, a published version. createPost/updatePost change the draft only. publishPost(id) copies the draft to the published version. unpublishPost(id) removes the published version; the draft stays. Queries read PUBLISHED by default. Pass stage: DRAFT to preview drafts (signed-in users only).

Admins enable it per content type (workflow: true, or the toggle in the admin UI). It's typically used for pages and blog posts. DRAFT ──submit──▶ IN_REVIEW ──approve──▶ PUBLISHED ▲ │ └─ CHANGES_REQUESTED ◀── request changes (comment required) Mutation Who Effect submitPostForReview(id) Contributor, Admin, Owner DRAFT or CHANGES_REQUESTED → IN_REVIEW. The draft must be valid. approvePost(id, comment) Reviewer, Admin, Owner IN_REVIEW → published (PUBLISHED) requestChangesPost(id, comment: String!) Reviewer, Admin, Owner IN_REVIEW → CHANGES_REQUESTED publishPost(id) Admin, Owner publish directly, bypassing review Contributors can't publish workflow types directly. On types without workflow, they publish themselves. Editing an entry (any updatePost) sets it back to DRAFT, also while it's in review. Reviewers therefore always approve exactly what gets published.

{ posts(stage: DRAFT, where: { workflowStatus: IN_REVIEW }) { items { title workflowStatus createdBy updatedBy history { action at by comment } # newest first } } } History actions: CREATED, UPDATED, SUBMITTED, CHANGES_REQUESTED, APPROVED, PUBLISHED, UNPUBLISHED. The last 50 events are kept. createdBy, updatedBy and history contain staff names, so they are null for anonymous readers. Plugins can react to submit, approve and requestChanges, for example to notify reviewers. See the plugin contract.

The same tess binary runs as a Lambda function when it detects the Lambda runtime. The SAM template deploy/aws/template.yaml deploys: the function: provided.al2023, arm64, built with cargo-lambda, exposed through a Function URL; a DynamoDB table (pk/sk, on-demand, point-in-time recovery, encryption); a private S3 bucket for media, with a CORS rule for browser uploads; environment variables resolved from AWS Secrets Manager.

Create the secrets (one random value each): aws secretsmanager create-secret --name tess/secrets --secret-string \ '{"adminToken":"…","idSecret":"…","refSecret":"…","sessionSecret":"…","typesenseApiKey":""}' Build and deploy (needs the SAM CLI and cargo-lambda): cd deploy/aws sam build --beta-features sam deploy --guided Parameters: SecretName (default tess/secrets), TypesenseUrl (empty disables search) and CorsOrigins. The ApiUrl output is your endpoint. Create the first Owner with the admin token (see Quick start), then remove adminToken from the secret and redeploy.

cargo lambda build --release --arm64 -p tess-server \ --no-default-features --features dynamodb,sql,lambda,s3 # output: target/lambda/tess/bootstrap :::warning arm64 cross-compilation Some zig versions fail to link aarch64 with unsupported linker arg: --fix-cortex-a53-843419. Use a zig release that supports the flag, or build with --x86-64 and set Architectures: [x86_64] in the template. :::

Startup: on a cold start, Tess runs migrations, loads the content model and the enabled plugins, and builds the GraphQL schema. Warm invocations reuse them, and changes made elsewhere are picked up within TESS_SCHEMA_REFRESH_SECS. Backends: RocksDB, SQLite and the filesystem media store are refused, because nothing on the Lambda filesystem persists. PostgreSQL works too (RDS, Aurora, Neon); the pool defaults to 2 connections per execution environment. Uploads: requests are limited to 6 MB by Lambda, so use direct uploads (createAssetUpload) for media; see Media storage. Logs are JSON, in CloudWatch. :::danger Secrets in environment variables The template resolves secrets into environment variables at deploy time. Anyone allowed to call lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration can read them, so restrict that permission. :::

Tess can cache public API responses in a server speaking the Redis protocol: Valkey, Redis, KeyDB, Dragonfly, or a managed service. Use the one your team already runs. The cache is optional: with TESS_CACHE=none (the default) nothing changes. TESS_CACHE=valkey # valkey, redis, keydb or dragonfly TESS_CACHE_URL=redis://valkey:6379 # rediss:// for TLS; redis://user:password@host:6379/0 TESS_CACHE_TTL_SECS=60 TESS_CACHE_PREFIX=tess: # to share one server between installs

They all work the same way for Tess: it only uses GET, SET … PX, INCR, PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE. TESS_CACHE names the server in the logs and in /health. Server TESS_CACHE Compose profile License Notes Valkey 8 valkey cache BSD 3-Clause Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2. The default here. Redis 8 redis cache-redis RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPLv3 Redis 6 and 7 work too. KeyDB 6.3 keydb cache-keydb BSD 3-Clause Multithreaded fork of Redis. Its last release is from 2023. Dragonfly 2 dragonfly cache-dragonfly BSL 1.1 Multithreaded, Redis-compatible; needs 256 MiB per thread. Managed service the engine's name See below. Licenses are given for information: check them with each vendor. All four are tested with Tess (TESS_TEST_CACHE_URL=… cargo test -p tess-cache). Not supported: cluster mode (Redis Cluster, ElastiCache "cluster mode enabled") and Sentinel. Use a single primary endpoint: a cache needs no sharding at this size, and a replica failover only empties it.

docker-compose.yml has a service for each server, in its own profile, with no persistence, a memory limit (CACHE_MAXMEMORY, default 256mb) and LRU eviction. Pick one: # Valkey TESS_CACHE=valkey TESS_CACHE_URL=redis://valkey:6379 # docker compose --profile cache up -d # Redis TESS_CACHE=redis TESS_CACHE_URL=redis://redis:6379 # docker compose --profile cache-redis up -d # KeyDB TESS_CACHE=keydb TESS_CACHE_URL=redis://keydb:6379 # docker compose --profile cache-keydb up -d # Dragonfly TESS_CACHE=dragonfly TESS_CACHE_URL=redis://dragonfly:6379 # docker compose --profile cache-dragonfly up -d scripts/init-env.sh --cache redis (or valkey, keydb, dragonfly) writes these settings and prints the matching command.

The services above, as docker run commands (any recent version works): docker run -d --name valkey -p 6379:6379 valkey/valkey:8-alpine \ valkey-server --save "" --appendonly no --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8-alpine \ redis-server --save "" --appendonly no --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru docker run -d --name keydb -p 6379:6379 eqalpha/keydb:latest \ keydb-server --save "" --appendonly no --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru docker run -d --name dragonfly -p 6379:6379 --ulimit memlock=-1 docker.dragonflydb.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly:v2.0.2 \ --cache_mode=true --maxmemory=256mb --proactor_threads=1 --dbfilename= With a password (requirepass, or an ACL user), put it in the URL: redis://:password@host:6379, or redis://user:password@host:6379. A database number goes at the end: redis://host:6379/2.

Service TESS_CACHE TESS_CACHE_URL Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey or Redis OSS, cluster mode disabled) valkey / redis rediss://:AUTH_TOKEN@master.my-cache.xxxxxx.euw1.cache.amazonaws.com:6379 (primary endpoint, with in-transit encryption) Amazon MemoryDB valkey / redis Not supported: MemoryDB always runs in cluster mode. Azure Cache for Redis redis rediss://:ACCESS_KEY@my-cache.redis.cache.windows.net:6380 Google Cloud Memorystore (Valkey or Redis) valkey / redis redis://10.0.0.3:6379 (private IP; rediss:// with in-transit encryption) Upstash redis rediss://default:PASSWORD@my-db.upstash.io:6379 Redis Cloud redis rediss://default:PASSWORD@redis-12345.c1.eu-west-1-2.ec2.redns.redis-cloud.com:12345 TLS (rediss://) checks the server certificate against the public CA roots.

Cached Key GraphQL queries by anonymous visitors (public reads, PUBLISHED content) ✔ query, operation name, variables Translation files served at /i18n/{format}/{file} ✔ format, file Requests with a token or session, mutations, responses with errors ✘ Responses carry an X-Tess-Cache header: HIT, MISS, or BYPASS when the cache server is unavailable. Drafts are never cached: anonymous visitors can only read published content, and signed-in requests always go to the database, so editors and previews always see the latest version.

You never purge the cache by hand. Every change invalidates it: Content: creating, updating, publishing, unpublishing or deleting an entry (from the admin UI, the API, MCP, plugins or imports), a change to a content model or component, and any successful mutation. Translations: any change to languages, keys or texts. Invalidation is instant and costs one command: each scope has a generation counter that is part of every key. Changing it makes all older entries unreachable, and they expire on their TTL.

With a cache server, all Tess instances share the cache: a response cached by one is served by the others, and a change on any instance invalidates it for all. The server also carries the content model changes (pub/sub): when one instance changes a model, the others rebuild their GraphQL schema at once instead of after the TESS_SCHEMA_REFRESH_SECS delay.

Give the server a memory limit and let it evict the least recently used keys: --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (Valkey, Redis, KeyDB), or --cache_mode=true --maxmemory=256mb (Dragonfly). volatile-lru works too. Persistence is not needed: an empty cache only means a few slower requests. Any eviction policy is safe. If a server evicts an invalidation counter, Tess restarts it from the current time, never from a value it had before, so entries cached earlier can't come back. TESS_CACHE_TTL_SECS is capped at half of TESS_MEDIA_URL_TTL_SECS and of TESS_ID_TTL, so cached responses never contain expired file URLs or ids.

Tess keeps working without it. Requests skip the cache (X-Tess-Cache: BYPASS) and a warning is logged. After a failure Tess waits 5 seconds before trying again, so requests don't wait on an unresponsive server. The cache is used again as soon as the server answers, and the other instances' schemas are refreshed in case a change was missed.

documents.t: TESS_CACHE=memory keeps the cache in the process (at most TESS_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES responses). It only suits a single instance: other instances would serve stale responses until the TTL.
Use a cache server (ElastiCache or Upstash) so that all concurrent Lambda instances share the cache and its invalidation.

Tess is configured only through environment variables. Secrets must come from the environment or a secrets manager, never from files committed to a repository. A commented template is provided as .env.example. Generate every secret with a fresh random value: openssl rand -hex 32

Variable Default Description TESS_LICENSE community community (personal use) or commercial (any commercial use, see Community & Enterprise). The commercial license excludes the embedded n8n workflow editor: TESS_N8N_URL is then ignored. TESS_LICENSE_KEY Required with commercial: your license key (tess_…). Tess refuses to start without a valid one. Never logged or returned by the API.

Variable Default Description TESS_ID_SECRET required Key encrypting the opaque API ids. At least 32 bytes. TESS_REF_SECRET required Key for stable ref values. At least 32 bytes, different from TESS_ID_SECRET. TESS_SESSION_SECRET required Key signing user sessions. At least 32 bytes. Changing it signs everybody out. TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN unset Bootstrap token with full access (acts as the "system" Owner). At least 32 characters. Use it to create the first Owner, then remove it. TESS_ID_SECRET_PREVIOUS unset Comma-separated previous id secrets, still accepted for decoding during a key rotation. TESS_ID_TTL 24h Lifetime of opaque ids (900s, 30m, 24h, 7d). TESS_SESSION_TTL 12h Lifetime of user sessions. TESS_SECRETS_KEY TESS_SESSION_SECRET Key encrypting integration secrets stored in the database (webhook signing secrets and headers, storage keys of translation delivery targets). At least 32 bytes. Changing it makes them unreadable: re-enter them.

Variable Default Description TESS_DATABASE memory postgres, mysql, sqlite, mongodb, dynamodb, rocksdb or memory. The Docker image sets rocksdb. DATABASE_URL For postgres, mysql, sqlite: postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db, mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db?ssl-mode=required, sqlite:///data/tess.db. Its scheme must match TESS_DATABASE. TESS_DB_MAX_CONNECTIONS 10 (2 on Lambda) SQL connection pool size. MONGODB_URL For mongodb. MONGODB_DATABASE tess MongoDB database name. DYNAMODB_TABLE tess DynamoDB table (key schema pk/sk). DYNAMODB_ENDPOINT unset Custom endpoint, e.g. DynamoDB Local. DYNAMODB_CREATE_TABLE false Create the table at startup if missing (local development). ROCKSDB_PATH data/rocksdb RocksDB directory. AWS credentials and region for DynamoDB come from the standard AWS chain: the IAM role of the function or task, AWS_* variables, or a profile. See Databases.

Variable Default Description TESS_MEDIA_STORE fs (s3 on Lambda) fs or s3. TESS_MEDIA_DIR data/media Directory for fs. TESS_S3_BUCKET Bucket for s3 (required). TESS_S3_ENDPOINT unset Endpoint of S3-compatible services (Garage, MinIO, R2…). TESS_S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT TESS_S3_ENDPOINT Endpoint as browsers reach it, for presigned file URLs, when Tess uses an internal one (e.g. http://garage:3900 in Docker, http://localhost:3900 or https://s3.example.com for browsers). TESS_S3_REGION from the AWS chain Region (Garage uses garage by default). TESS_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE true when an endpoint is set Path-style URLs, needed by most self-hosted services. TESS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID / TESS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY unset Explicit credentials. Set both, or neither to use the default AWS chain. TESS_S3_CREATE_BUCKET false Create the bucket at startup if missing. TESS_MEDIA_PUBLIC_URL unset Public base URL (CDN) of the bucket: asset URLs become {base}/{key}. TESS_MEDIA_URL_TTL_SECS 3600 Lifetime of presigned upload/download URLs. TESS_MEDIA_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES 104857600 (100 MiB) Maximum file size. See Media storage.

Variable Default Description TESS_SEARCH none none, typesense or memory. TYPESENSE_URL e.g. http://typesense:8108. TYPESENSE_API_KEY Typesense admin API key. TYPESENSE_COLLECTION_PREFIX tess_ Prefix of collection names, to share a cluster. See Search.

Variable Default Description TESS_CACHE none none, memory (one instance), or a server shared by every instance: valkey, redis, keydb or dragonfly (any server speaking the Redis protocol works). TESS_CACHE_URL redis://[user:password@]host:6379/0, or rediss:// for TLS. VALKEY_URL and REDIS_URL are read too. TESS_CACHE_TTL_SECS 60 Lifetime of cached responses; capped at half of TESS_MEDIA_URL_TTL_SECS and TESS_ID_TTL. TESS_CACHE_PREFIX tess: Prefix of keys and channels, to share a server between installs. TESS_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES 10000 memory only. See Cache.

Variable Default Description TESS_PLUGINS true Enable the WebAssembly plugin system. TESS_PLUGIN_ALLOW_HTTP true Whether admins may allow plugins to make HTTP requests at all. TESS_PLUGIN_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS 10000 Highest per-plugin timeout an admin can set (plugins default to 1000 ms). TESS_PLUGIN_MAX_MEMORY_PAGES 1024 (64 MiB) Highest per-plugin memory cap, in 64 KiB pages (plugins default to 256 = 16 MiB). TESS_PLUGIN_MAX_MODULE_BYTES 20971520 (20 MiB) Maximum module size.

Variable Default Description TESS_I18N true Enable translations (API, /i18n/{format}/{file}, delivery targets). TESS_WEBHOOKS true Enable webhooks. TESS_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS unset (any) Comma-separated hosts webhooks may target (*.example.com allowed). TESS_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS 10 Timeout of one delivery attempt. TESS_WEBHOOK_MAX_ATTEMPTS 5 Attempts per delivery (retries after 10 s, 1 min, 5 min, 30 min). On AWS Lambda: one inline attempt. TESS_N8N_URL unset Where Tess reaches n8n, e.g. http://n8n:5678. Enables the /n8n/ proxy and the admin Workflows page. Not on AWS Lambda. TESS_N8N_PATH /n8n/ Path the n8n editor is served under; n8n must use the same N8N_PATH. TESS_FORMS true Enable forms (API, GET/POST /api/forms/<slug>). TESS_FORMS_RATE_LIMIT 10 Submissions accepted per visitor and form, per minute. TESS_CALENDARS true Enable calendars: linked Google calendars and cal.diy booking pages. TESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, TESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET unset Google OAuth client for calendars. Without them, Admins set one in the admin (stored encrypted). CALDIY_PUBLIC_URL, CALDIY_DB_PASSWORD, CALDIY_NEXTAUTH_SECRET, CALDIY_ENCRYPTION_KEY The caldiy Compose profile: see Calendars.

documents.t: Variable Default Description PORT 8080 HTTP port (ignored on Lambda). TESS_PUBLIC_READ true Anonymous requests may read PUBLISHED content. TESS_CORS_ORIGINS * Comma-separated allowed origins, or *. TESS_GRAPHIQL true Serve the GraphiQL IDE on GET /graphql. TESS_INTROSPECTION true GraphQL introspection (the admin UI's review queue uses it). TESS_DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE 100 Default first of list queries. TESS_MAX_PAGE_SIZE 1000 Maximum first of list queries. TESS_MAX_QUERY_DEPTH 16 Maximum GraphQL query depth. TESS_SCHEMA_REFRESH_SECS 10 How often an instance checks for model and plugin changes made elsewhere. TESS_ADMIN_DIR admin/dist/client if present Directory of the built admin UI, served under /admin/.
Variable Default Description RUST_LOG info Log filter, e.g. info,tess_graphql=debug. TESS_LOG_FORMAT text (json on Lambda) Set to json for structured logs.

The tess-server package has one cargo feature per backend, so you can build smaller binaries: Feature Enables sql (aliases postgres, mysql, sqlite) the SQL backend mongodb MongoDB dynamodb DynamoDB rocksdb RocksDB (needs clang and cmake to build) s3 S3-compatible media store lambda AWS Lambda runtime All are on by default. For example: cargo build --release -p tess-server --no-default-features --features sql,s3 # binary: target/release/tess Choosing a backend that the binary was built without fails at startup with a clear message.

Select a backend with TESS_DATABASE. Every backend passes the same conformance test suite, so filters, sorting, pagination, draft/publish, users and settings behave identically on all of them. Tables, collections and indexes are created automatically at startup. Migrations are idempotent and safe to run concurrently; on PostgreSQL they are serialized with an advisory lock. Backend TESS_DATABASE Instances Filtering Best for PostgreSQL postgres many in SQL general production use MySQL 8 mysql many in SQL existing MySQL infrastructure SQLite sqlite one in SQL single-container installs MongoDB mongodb many in MongoDB existing MongoDB infrastructure DynamoDB dynamodb many in memory (per type) AWS Lambda, serverless RocksDB rocksdb one in memory (per type) embedded, zero-dependency Memory memory one in memory tests and demos; data is lost on restart

One backend built with SeaQuery serves all three. DATABASE_URL selects the engine, and its scheme must match TESS_DATABASE. TESS_DATABASE=postgres DATABASE_URL=postgres://tess:CHANGE_ME@db.example.com:5432/tess TESS_DATABASE=mysql DATABASE_URL='mysql://tess:CHANGE_ME@db.example.com:3306/tess?ssl-mode=required' TESS_DATABASE=sqlite DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///data/tess.db Tables: tess_content_type, tess_entry (one JSON document per stage) and tess_setting (users, API tokens, plugins). The pool size is TESS_DB_MAX_CONNECTIONS. :::warning MySQL 8 requires TLS MySQL 8's default authentication (caching_sha2_password) needs either TLS or RSA key exchange, and Tess doesn't enable the RSA option. Add ?ssl-mode=required to the URL. ::: SQLite runs in WAL mode with a busy timeout. Keep the file on a persistent volume, and run a single instance. Collations: string comparison and sorting are bytewise on every engine, whatever the database's default collation. Key columns use utf8mb4_bin on MySQL. Performance: filters are evaluated on the JSON documents of one content type, without dedicated indexes. This is fine for most sites; very large types will benefit from future generated indexes.
TESS_DATABASE=mongodb MONGODB_URL=mongodb://mongo.example.com:27017 MONGODB_DATABASE=tess Collections: tess_content_types, tess_entries, tess_settings. Filters and sorting run in MongoDB.

Single-table design: pk sk doc CT content type apiId content type JSON E#{apiId} entry uuid entry JSON S setting key setting JSON TESS_DATABASE=dynamodb DYNAMODB_TABLE=tess The table needs string keys pk (partition) and sk (sort). On-demand billing is recommended; the SAM template creates it. The IAM role needs CRUD access to the table (GetItem, PutItem, DeleteItem, Query, BatchWriteItem; plus DescribeTable/CreateTable if you use DYNAMODB_CREATE_TABLE). info List queries read the whole partition of a content type, then filter and sort in memory. That suits thousands of entries per type; beyond that, put a cache or CDN in front or choose a SQL backend. Items are limited to 400 KB by DynamoDB.

TESS_DATABASE=rocksdb ROCKSDB_PATH=/data/rocksdb An embedded key-value store: no service to run, one process only (the directory is locked), and not usable on Lambda. Filtering is done in memory per content type.
There's no built-in migration tool between backends yet. Choose the backend before going to production.

The Dockerfile builds Tess in three stages: the admin UI (Node), the server (Rust), and a slim Debian runtime image. docker build -t tess . # Smaller image with only some backends: docker build --build-arg FEATURES=sql,s3 -t tess:sql . Binary /usr/local/bin/tess User tess (uid 10001), non-root Admin UI /app/admin, served at /admin/ Volume /data (RocksDB database and local media) Port 8080 Defaults TESS_DATABASE=rocksdb, ROCKSDB_PATH=/data/rocksdb, TESS_MEDIA_STORE=fs, TESS_MEDIA_DIR=/data/media, TESS_LOG_FORMAT=json The build argument FEATURES selects the cargo features (default: sql,mongodb,dynamodb,rocksdb,s3).

docker-compose.yml runs Tess alone by default: content in an embedded RocksDB database and uploaded files on disk, both in the tess-data volume. Optional services are profiles, and scripts/init-env.sh writes a .env for the ones you pick. scripts/init-env.sh -y # Tess alone docker compose up -d --build

The local profile adds every service Tess can use, self-hosted next to it: Garage (S3 media), Typesense (search), Valkey (cache) and n8n (workflows). init-env.sh --local writes the matching .env, secrets included: scripts/init-env.sh --local docker compose --profile local up -d --build Garage is set up automatically: the garage-init service creates its layout, the TESS_S3_BUCKET bucket and the TESS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID key at every start (it's idempotent), and Tess starts once it's done. Media URLs use TESS_S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT (http://localhost:3900), the Garage port published for your browser. Add a database profile if you want one, e.g. --profile local --profile postgres. With the commercial license, which doesn't include the embedded n8n editor, use local-commercial instead: the same services without n8n. scripts/init-env.sh --local --license commercial # then fill TESS_LICENSE_KEY in .env docker compose --profile local-commercial up -d --build
