cp .env.example .env # Fill TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN, TESS_ID_SECRET, TESS_REF_SECRET, TESS_SESSION_SECRET # (one `openssl rand -hex 32` each), plus the passwords of the profiles you use. docker compose --profile postgres --profile search up -d --build Open http://localhost:8080/admin/ and create the first Owner with the bootstrap token. Remove TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN from .env. Run docker compose up -d again to apply it. tip Put Tess behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS (Caddy, Traefik, nginx), and set TESS_CORS_ORIGINS to your front-end origins. See Security.

Garage needs a one-time setup: a cluster layout, a bucket and an access key. With the s3 and local profiles, the garage-init service does it through Garage's admin API (deploy/garage/setup.sh) from these .env settings: TESS_S3_BUCKET=tess-media TESS_S3_ENDPOINT=http://garage:3900 # how Tess reaches Garage TESS_S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:3900 # how browsers reach it (file URLs) TESS_S3_REGION=garage TESS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=GK… # GK + 24 hex: "GK$(openssl rand -hex 12)" TESS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=… # 64 hex: openssl rand -hex 32 GARAGE_RPC_SECRET=… # openssl rand -hex 32 GARAGE_ADMIN_TOKEN=… # openssl rand -hex 32 init-env.sh generates them. Garage's own configuration is deploy/garage/garage.toml. For a Garage outside Compose, deploy/garage/init.sh <container> <bucket> <key-id> <key-secret> does the same through docker exec.

cargo build --release -p tess-server # needs clang + cmake for RocksDB (cd admin && npm ci && npm run build) # optional: the admin UI TESS_ADMIN_DIR=admin/dist/client ./target/release/tess For a quick throwaway instance (in-memory database, random secrets), use scripts/dev-server.sh.

tess-transfer copies content models and users between Tess instances: from development to production, into a fresh install, or into version control (models only). It talks to the GraphQL API, so it works with every deployment (Docker, Lambda…) and every database. It's shipped in the Docker image next to tess, or you can build it with cargo build --release -p tess-transfer. export TESS_URL=https://cms.example.com export TESS_TOKEN=… # Admin role: session token, API token or bootstrap token tess-transfer export -o tess.yaml # models + users tess-transfer export --only models -o models.json # JSON, models only tess-transfer import tess.yaml --dry-run # show the plan tess-transfer import tess.yaml --passwords-out new-users.txt tess-transfer import models.yaml --update # also replace existing models The token is read from TESS_TOKEN only, never from the command line, so it doesn't end up in your shell history. Importing Owners requires an Owner token.
documents.s: Importing and exporting models and users

documents.t: YAML or JSON, chosen from the file extension (.yaml, .yml, .json) or with --format yaml|json. Defaults are omitted. version: 1 components: - apiId: Seo fields: - {name: metaTitle, type: TEXT, maxLength: 60} - {name: metaDescription, type: TEXT, maxLength: null} # null = unlimited contentTypes: - apiId: Post pluralApiId: posts # optional description: Blog posts # optional workflow: true # optional (default false) fields: - {name: title, type: TEXT, required: true, maxLength: 120} - {name: status, type: ENUM, enumValues: [DRAFTED, LIVE]} - {name: cover, type: RELATION, relationTarget: Asset} - {name: tags, type: RELATION, relationTarget: Tag, many: true} - {name: seo, type: COMPONENT, component: Seo} - apiId: Tag fields: - {name: label, type: TEXT} users: - email: ada@example.com name: Ada Example role: ADMIN # OWNER, ADMIN, CONTRIBUTOR, REVIEWER, MEMBER scope: [Post] # optional, for Contributors and Reviewers disabled: false # optional # password: … # optional, import only; never exported Unknown keys are rejected, with their line and column.

Validation first. The whole file is checked against the server before anything changes: duplicates, relations to unknown content types, missing emails or roles, and the passwords file. Models in any order. Components are created before content types, nested components before the components containing them. Models can reference each other in cycles (Post ↔ Tag): relations to models that don't exist yet are added in a second pass. maxLength of TEXT fields: absent means the server default (80), null means unlimited. Exports always write it. Existing models and users are skipped, unless you pass --update: Models: their definition is replaced, exactly like an edit in the admin. Users: their name, role, scope and status are updated. Passwords are never changed. The built-in Asset type is never exported or imported. Passwords: exports never contain them, since only hashes exist on the server. New users without a password get a random one, written to the --passwords-out file (mode 600) and never printed. Share each password privately, ask users to change it, and delete the file. Errors: each failure is reported, and the exit code is non-zero when anything failed. :::warning Personal data A file with users contains staff email addresses. Keep it out of version control and delete it after use. Model-only exports (--only models) are safe to commit. :::

docker compose exec -e TESS_TOKEN tess tess-transfer export --only models > models.yaml docker compose exec -T -e TESS_TOKEN tess tess-transfer import - --format yaml < models.yaml (TESS_URL defaults to http://localhost:8080, which is the server itself inside the container.)
Uploaded files (and plugin modules) are stored in a blob store. Their metadata lives in the database, as entries of the built-in Asset content type.

TESS_MEDIA_STORE=fs TESS_MEDIA_DIR=/data/media Files are served by Tess at /media/files/{key}. Keys contain 128 random bits (assets/<random>/<file-name>), and responses carry X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox, so uploaded HTML or SVG can't run scripts in your origin. Use this store with one instance only, on a persistent volume.

TESS_MEDIA_STORE=s3 TESS_S3_BUCKET=tess-media TESS_S3_ENDPOINT=http://garage:3900 # omit for AWS S3 TESS_S3_REGION=garage TESS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=GK… # omit both to use the AWS chain (IAM role) TESS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=… When TESS_S3_ENDPOINT is set, path-style URLs are used (TESS_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE), as most self-hosted services require. To create the bucket at startup, set TESS_S3_CREATE_BUCKET=true. File URLs are presigned for the endpoint. When Tess reaches the store through an internal address that browsers can't (http://garage:3900 inside Docker Compose), set TESS_S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT to the address browsers use, e.g. http://localhost:3900 or https://s3.example.com. Tess keeps talking to TESS_S3_ENDPOINT, and signs download and direct-upload URLs for the public one.
documents.s: S3-compatible (Garage, MinIO, AWS S3, Cloudflare R2…)

documents.t: With S3 stores, clients can upload straight to the bucket with a presigned PUT (createAssetUpload → upload → confirmAssetUpload, see Media for developers). This avoids proxying large files through Tess, and bypasses the 6 MB request limit of AWS Lambda. Browsers then need a CORS rule on the bucket, for example: [{ "AllowedMethods": ["PUT", "GET"], "AllowedOrigins": ["https://admin.example.com"], "AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "MaxAgeSeconds": 3600 }]

Asset.url is computed in this order: TESS_MEDIA_PUBLIC_URL is set (a CDN or public bucket): the URL is {TESS_MEDIA_PUBLIC_URL}/{key}. Otherwise, the store supports presigning: a presigned GET URL, valid TESS_MEDIA_URL_TTL_SECS seconds. Otherwise: /media/files/{key}, served by Tess.

Size limit: files over TESS_MEDIA_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (default 100 MiB) are rejected. Deletion: deleting an Asset entry deletes its file. Plugin modules are stored in the same store under plugins/, with their SHA-256 checksum verified on load. Back them up together with your database (see Operations).

curl -s http://localhost:8080/health # {"status":"ok","storage":"postgres"} The endpoint returns 200 when the database answers, and 503 otherwise. Use it for container health checks and load-balancer probes.

Format: text logs by default; set TESS_LOG_FORMAT=json for structured logs. Logs are always JSON on Lambda. Verbosity: control it with RUST_LOG, e.g. RUST_LOG=info,tower_http=debug. Notable events: schema rebuilds, plugin loads and failures, storage errors (clients only see "internal storage error"), and account lockouts.

Tess keeps everything in two places. Back up both, consistently: The database: content types, entries, users, API tokens, plugin settings. The media store: uploaded files and plugin modules. Backend Suggested backup PostgreSQL pg_dump, or managed snapshots / PITR MySQL mysqldump --single-transaction, or managed snapshots SQLite sqlite3 tess.db ".backup backup.db" (safe while running) MongoDB mongodump, or managed snapshots DynamoDB point-in-time recovery (enabled by the SAM template) RocksDB stop Tess and copy the directory, or snapshot the volume S3 / Garage bucket versioning or replication Filesystem media copy or snapshot TESS_MEDIA_DIR To copy only the content models and users to another instance (e.g. from staging to production), use tess-transfer. After restoring, run reindexSearch if you use Typesense (see Search).
Back up. Deploy the new version. Schema migrations run automatically at startup and are idempotent.

Run several instances against a shared network database and an S3 bucket. Model and plugin changes reach every instance within TESS_SCHEMA_REFRESH_SECS. RocksDB, SQLite and filesystem media are single-instance only.

The repository contains the full test suite, including conformance tests against real PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB Local, Garage and Typesense started in throwaway containers: scripts/test-all.sh # needs Docker NO_CONTAINERS=1 scripts/test-all.sh # without external services

Tess is one binary, tess, that serves the GraphQL API, the REST upload endpoints, the health check and the admin UI. When it detects the AWS Lambda runtime (AWS_LAMBDA_RUNTIME_API is set), it runs as a Lambda function; otherwise it starts an HTTP server on PORT (default 8080). GET/POST /graphql GraphQL API (GraphiQL IDE on GET, if enabled) GET /graphql/schema.graphql current schema (SDL) POST /media/upload file upload (Contributor or above) GET /media/files/{key} file download (filesystem media store) POST /api/plugins/{name} plugin module upload (Admin or above) GET /admin/ admin UI GET /health health check GET /favicon.svg the Tess logo Everything else is pluggable and chosen by configuration: Concern Options Page Database PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, SQLite, MongoDB, DynamoDB, RocksDB, memory Databases Media files local filesystem, S3-compatible (Garage, MinIO, AWS S3, R2…) Media storage Full-text search none, Typesense, memory Search Plugins on/off, sandbox limits Security, Plugins

Deployment Good for Typical stack Docker / Compose most self-hosted installs tess + PostgreSQL (or SQLite) + Garage + Typesense. See Docker. Single VM small installs the tess binary under systemd, SQLite or RocksDB, filesystem media Raspberry Pi home servers, tiny devices the arm64 or armv7 binary under systemd, RocksDB or SQLite. See Raspberry Pi & small devices. Kubernetes several replicas the Docker image as a Deployment, with PostgreSQL/MySQL/MongoDB and S3 AWS Lambda serverless, pay per use DynamoDB + S3 (+ Typesense Cloud). See AWS Lambda. Phusion Passenger hosts that only run Ruby/Node apps tess started and proxied by a Rack config.ru, RocksDB/SQLite or a managed database. See Phusion Passenger. :::warning Single-instance backends RocksDB, SQLite and the filesystem media store live on a local disk. Use them with exactly one instance, and with a persistent volume. Tess refuses to start with them on AWS Lambda. For several replicas, use a network database and an S3-compatible bucket. :::

Instances share nothing but the database, the media store and the search engine. When an admin changes a content model or a plugin, the instance that handled the request applies it immediately. The others pick it up within TESS_SCHEMA_REFRESH_SECS (default 10 s), which also applies to separate Lambda execution environments.
Configuration reference Docker, AWS Lambda, Phusion Passenger or Raspberry Pi Security checklist Operations: health, logs, backups, upgrades

Some hosts (shared hosting, cPanel/Plesk "Ruby/Node.js app" features) only run applications through Phusion Passenger. Passenger cannot start a Rust binary itself, but it runs Ruby (Rack) apps, so Tess ships a small Rack launcher, config.ru: browser ──▶ Passenger ──┬─▶ public/admin/… static admin UI (served by Passenger) └─▶ config.ru (rack-proxy) ──▶ tess on 127.0.0.1:18080 Passenger serves the prebuilt admin UI directly from public/admin/: it is a static (SSG) site and needs no application server. Every other request (/graphql, /media/*, /api/*, /health, admin client-side routes that are not files) goes to config.ru, which starts the tess binary on localhost, restarts it if it exits, and proxies to it with rack-proxy.

Passenger 6 with Ruby 3.1 or later and Bundler. The right to run a binary from your app folder (ask your host: some shared plans forbid executables or long-running child processes). A tess binary for the host's platform, usually Linux x86_64. Build on a matching machine, in Docker, or with TARGET=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu. Settings that keep exactly one app process alive (see below).

config.ru and its Gemfile live in deploy/passenger/. Every cargo build -p tess-server copies them next to the binary, so target/release/ already holds tess, config.ru and Gemfile. The packaging script also builds the admin UI and assembles the folder to upload: scripts/package-passenger.sh # backends to compile in, and a cross target: FEATURES=sql,rocksdb,s3 TARGET=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu scripts/package-passenger.sh dist/passenger/ (also dist/passenger.tar.gz) ├── config.ru ├── Gemfile ├── tess ├── public/admin/ admin UI ├── log/ tess.log ├── tmp/ lock file └── data/ RocksDB / SQLite / media, if stored locally

Upload the folder (or the tarball) as the application root, then: cd ~/apps/tess chmod +x tess bundle config set --local path vendor/bundle bundle install Point the domain's document root at public/ (Passenger apps always serve <app root>/public statically).

Tess must run as one process that Passenger never stops: config.ru supervises a single tess child, and the embedded backends (RocksDB, SQLite, filesystem media) do not support several processes. Also use direct spawning, so the child is not started in Passenger's preloader. Nginx integration: server { server_name cms.example.com; root /home/me/apps/tess/public; passenger_enabled on; passenger_app_type rack; passenger_spawn_method direct; passenger_min_instances 1; passenger_max_pool_size 1; passenger_pool_idle_time 0; passenger_max_request_queue_size 200; client_max_body_size 100m; # media uploads, see TESS_MEDIA_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES passenger_env_var TESS_DATABASE rocksdb; passenger_env_var ROCKSDB_PATH /home/me/apps/tess/data/rocksdb; passenger_env_var TESS_MEDIA_DIR /home/me/apps/tess/data/media; passenger_env_var TESS_ID_SECRET …; passenger_env_var TESS_REF_SECRET …; passenger_env_var TESS_SESSION_SECRET …; passenger_env_var TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN …; # first run only } # Keep the app (and tess) running after a restart, without waiting for a request: passenger_pre_start https://cms.example.com/health; Apache integration (.htaccess or virtual host): PassengerEnabled on PassengerAppType rack PassengerSpawnMethod direct PassengerMinInstances 1 PassengerMaxPoolSize 1 PassengerPoolIdleTime 0 SetEnv TESS_DATABASE rocksdb SetEnv ROCKSDB_PATH /home/me/apps/tess/data/rocksdb SetEnv TESS_ID_SECRET … # … other variables On control panels (cPanel "Setup Ruby App", Plesk), set the application root, config.ru as the startup file, and the variables in the environment section. If you cannot change the pool settings, ask your host, or see Running tess separately. Every configuration variable is passed to tess through the environment of the Ruby process. Never put secrets in files inside the app folder. config.ru itself reads: Variable Default Description TESS_INTERNAL_PORT 18080 Local port tess listens on (PORT of the child). Change it if the port is taken. TESS_BIN <app root>/tess Path of the binary. TESS_ADMIN_DIR <app root>/public/admin Admin UI folder, used by tess for client-side routes. TESS_LOG_FILE <app root>/log/tess.log Output of tess.

Database: RocksDB or SQLite in data/ (one instance, on a disk that is backed up), or a managed PostgreSQL/MySQL if your host provides one. See Databases. Media: TESS_MEDIA_STORE=fs with TESS_MEDIA_DIR in data/, or any S3-compatible bucket. See Media storage.

Restart the app (touch tmp/restart.txt or the panel's restart button). Check https://cms.example.com/health: it answers {"status":"ok",…}. Open https://cms.example.com/admin/, sign in with TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN and create the Owner account. Remove TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN and restart.
Upload the new tess binary and public/admin/ folder, then restart the app. tess migrates the database at startup. Back up data/ first; see Operations.

Symptom Check 502 {"error":"tess is starting or unavailable"} log/tess.log: missing secrets, wrong binary platform (exec format error), port taken (change TESS_INTERNAL_PORT). 413 Request Entity Too Large on uploads client_max_body_size (Nginx) or LimitRequestBody (Apache). RocksDB "lock" errors Several app processes: set the pool to one process and direct spawning. The admin loads but data never appears The document root must be public/, and /graphql must reach config.ru. Restarts after idle periods are slow passenger_pool_idle_time 0 and passenger_pre_start.

One instance. Passenger cannot scale Tess horizontally here. Use Docker or AWS Lambda for several replicas. Buffered responses. rack-proxy runs with streaming: false, so each response is buffered before it is sent. Regular GraphQL, upload and media requests are fine, but long-lived streams (server-sent events) are not supported through this proxy.

If your host lets you keep a process running by other means (systemd user units, supervisord, a process manager in the panel), start tess that way on 127.0.0.1:$TESS_INTERNAL_PORT. config.ru then finds it already listening, does not start a second one, and only proxies. This is more robust, because tess no longer depends on Passenger's process lifecycle.

Tess is a single Rust binary with an embedded database. It doesn't need a JVM, Node.js or a database server, so it runs well on small ARM boards like the Raspberry Pi 3, 4 and 5. Tess's creator runs their own Tess on a Raspberry Pi 3, without n8n. On a PC, a fresh Tess with RocksDB or SQLite uses about 30 MB of memory while idle. It needs more as your content, traffic and plugins grow, but the CMS itself leaves most of a Pi free.

Board Memory Suggested setup Raspberry Pi 3 (B, B+, A+) 512 MB – 1 GB Tess alone: the native binary under systemd, RocksDB or SQLite, files on disk. No n8n, Typesense or PostgreSQL. Raspberry Pi 4 1 – 8 GB Tess alone on 1–2 GB. Docker Compose works well. Add n8n or PostgreSQL from 4 GB. Raspberry Pi 5 2 – 16 GB Docker Compose. From 4 GB, room for n8n, PostgreSQL, a cache server and Typesense. What uses the memory is the optional services, not Tess: n8n is a Node.js application and needs several hundred MB by itself. On a Pi 3, leave it off: Tess's webhooks can still call an n8n (or any other service) running on another machine. Typesense keeps its index in memory. On a Pi 3, keep TESS_SEARCH=none, or memory for a small site (that index is rebuilt after each restart, see Search). cal.diy is built from source, which needs about 6 GB of memory. Don't build it on a Pi. A cal.diy calendar only needs its webhook to reach Tess, so cal.diy can run anywhere.

A 64-bit OS is best: Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit), Debian or Ubuntu. The Pi 3, 4 and 5 all support it. glibc 2.35 or later: Raspberry Pi OS 12 "Bookworm" or later, or Ubuntu 22.04 or later. Raspberry Pi OS 11 "Bullseye" is too old for the release binaries. A good storage device. The database writes often, and cheap SD cards are slow and wear out. Prefer an A2-rated card, or a USB SSD (the Pi 4 and 5 boot from USB, the Pi 5 also from an NVMe HAT). Check what you have: uname -m # aarch64: 64-bit (arm64); armv7l: 32-bit (armv7) ldd --version # first line ends with the glibc version

Every release has native Linux archives: arm64 for 64-bit systems, armv7 for 32-bit ones. They hold tess, tess-transfer and the admin UI. VERSION=0.1.1 # the release you want ARCH=arm64 # or armv7 on a 32-bit OS curl -LO https://github.com/tessheadless/core/releases/download/v$VERSION/tess-$VERSION-linux-$ARCH.tar.xz curl -LO https://github.com/tessheadless/core/releases/download/v$VERSION/SHA256SUMS sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing sudo useradd --system --home /opt/tess --shell /usr/sbin/nologin tess sudo mkdir -p /opt/tess sudo tar -xJf tess-$VERSION-linux-$ARCH.tar.xz -C /opt/tess --strip-components=1 Create the configuration from the template, with random secrets: cd /opt/tess sudo cp .env.example .env for key in TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN TESS_SESSION_SECRET TESS_ID_SECRET TESS_REF_SECRET TESS_SECRETS_KEY; do sudo sed -i "s|^$key=.*|$key=$(openssl rand -hex 32)|" .env done sudo mkdir -p /opt/tess/data sudo chown -R tess:tess /opt/tess sudo chmod 600 /opt/tess/.env The defaults already suit a small device: RocksDB in data/rocksdb, uploads in data/media, no search engine, no cache and no n8n. To use SQLite instead, set TESS_DATABASE=sqlite and DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///opt/tess/data/tess.db?mode=rwc (it can be backed up while running). Run it as a systemd service, /etc/systemd/system/tess.service: [Unit] Description=Tess headless CMS After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] User=tess Group=tess WorkingDirectory=/opt/tess EnvironmentFile=/opt/tess/.env ExecStart=/opt/tess/tess Restart=on-failure NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true ReadWritePaths=/opt/tess/data PrivateTmp=true [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now tess curl http://localhost:8080/health journalctl -u tess -f # logs Then open http://<your-pi>:8080/admin/, sign in with TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN (sudo grep TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN /opt/tess/.env), create the Owner account, empty TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN in .env and run sudo systemctl restart tess. Upgrading: extract the new archive over /opt/tess (your .env and data/ are kept), then sudo systemctl restart tess.
documents.s: Install the native binary (recommended on a Pi 3)

documents.t: The Docker images are published for arm64, so the Docker guide works on a Pi with a 64-bit OS: download the arm64 Compose bundle and follow the same steps. On a 2 GB board, start Tess alone, then add the profiles you need, one at a time. There is no 32-bit (armv7) Docker image: on a 32-bit OS, use the native binary.

Don't build Tess on the Pi. Compiling RocksDB and the rest of Tess takes a long time and can run out of memory on a 1 GB board. Use the release archives, or cross-compile on a PC for aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu (.github/workflows/release.yml shows the toolchains used). Cache: TESS_CACHE=memory speeds up repeated public queries at almost no cost. Lower TESS_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES (default 10,000) if memory is tight. HTTPS and public access: put a reverse proxy like Caddy or nginx in front of port 8080, or reach the Pi through a VPN or a tunnel instead of opening a port on your router. See the security checklist. Back up /opt/tess/.env and /opt/tess/data to another machine. An SD card can fail without warning. See Backups.
Full-text search is optional. With TESS_SEARCH=none (the default), the search<Plural> queries are simply not generated.

TESS_SEARCH=typesense TYPESENSE_URL=http://typesense:8108 TYPESENSE_API_KEY=… # admin key, from your secrets manager TYPESENSE_COLLECTION_PREFIX=tess_ Opt-in per model: an Admin (or the Owner) enables search on each content type in Admin → Search and picks the indexed fields. A model needs at least one selected TEXT or MARKDOWN field; only enabled models get a search<Plural> query. Collections: Tess creates one collection per enabled content type (<prefix><ApiId>). Saving the settings rebuilds it from the database; disabling search drops it. Field schema: generated from each field's type (the admin page shows the result): Field type Typesense field Notes TEXT, MARKDOWN string Searched by queries ENUM, UUID, single RELATION string, facet Exact value; relations hold entry UUIDs RELATION (many) string[], facet INT int64, sortable FLOAT float, sortable BOOLEAN bool, facet DATE, DATETIME int64, sortable Unix seconds (DATE at midnight UTC) JSON, components and dynamic zones can't be indexed, and passwords never are. Every collection also has a stage facet (draft / published). What gets indexed: the draft and published versions are separate documents (draft_<uuid>, published_<uuid>), so published content is never mixed with drafts. When indexing happens: on every create, update, publish, unpublish and delete, inside the same request. Changing a content type rebuilds its collection; fields removed from the model leave the index. Results are loaded from the database, so they always match stored content. To share one Typesense cluster between installs, give each install its own prefix.

After restoring a backup, pointing Tess at a new Typesense cluster, or if the index looks out of date, rebuild it with an Admin token: mutation { reindexSearch } # every model with search enabled mutation { reindexSearch(apiId: "Post") } # one type The mutation returns the number of entries indexed. The admin page has a Reindex button per model, and the settings are available through the API: query { searchSettings { engine models { apiId enabled active fields { name type selected indexType engineConfig } } } } mutation { updateSearchSettings(apiId: "Post", enabled: true, fields: ["title", "body", "category"]) { active indexedEntries } }

TESS_SEARCH=memory keeps a naive index in the process. It's handy for tests and demos, but it's empty after every restart (run reindexSearch), and each instance has its own. The per-model settings are kept in the database.

Secrets: TESS_ID_SECRET, TESS_REF_SECRET and TESS_SESSION_SECRET are random (openssl rand -hex 32), different from each other, and stored in a secrets manager. Bootstrap token: the first Owner exists and TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN is removed. Tess logs a warning while it's set. TLS: a reverse proxy or load balancer terminates TLS (Tess speaks plain HTTP). CORS: TESS_CORS_ORIGINS lists your front-end and admin origins instead of *. Public read: decide whether anonymous clients may read published content (TESS_PUBLIC_READ). GraphiQL: TESS_GRAPHIQL=false in production, if you don't want the IDE exposed. Introspection (TESS_INTROSPECTION) is used by the admin UI's review queue. Limits: TESS_MAX_PAGE_SIZE and TESS_MAX_QUERY_DEPTH fit your use. Plugin network access: TESS_PLUGIN_ALLOW_HTTP=false if plugins never need it. Backups of the database and the media store (see Operations).

Credential Format Lifetime Revocation User session tess_s1.… TESS_SESSION_TTL (12 h) immediate: role/scope/status/password change, "sign out everywhere", deleting the user, or rotating TESS_SESSION_SECRET (everyone) API token tess_t1_… optional expiry revoke in the admin or with revokeApiToken Bootstrap token TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN while configured remove it from the configuration Passwords are hashed with Argon2id and need at least 12 characters. Lockout: after 10 failed sign-ins, an account is locked for 15 minutes. Login errors don't reveal whether an account exists. Sessions are stateless and signed. Every request reloads the user, so revocation takes effect immediately on every instance, Lambda included. API token secrets are shown once; only a SHA-256 hash is stored. Roles and what they allow are described in Authentication.
Entry ids in the API are encrypted (XChaCha20-Poly1305), type-bound, and expire after TESS_ID_TTL. Database ids never leave the server, not even to plugins.

Move the current secret to TESS_ID_SECRET_PREVIOUS and set a new TESS_ID_SECRET. Old ids keep working until they expire. After TESS_ID_TTL, remove the previous secret. TESS_REF_SECRET should not be rotated casually: every ref changes, and clients that cache by ref lose their keys.

Plugins are WebAssembly modules running in a sandbox with: No access to the filesystem or environment variables. Limits: a timeout and a memory cap. Network: none unless an admin lists allowed hosts, and never if TESS_PLUGIN_ALLOW_HTTP=false. Integrity: a SHA-256 checksum, verified when the module is loaded. Only Admins and Owners can install plugins, and they're installed disabled. Treat third-party modules like any dependency: review their source and their requested hosts. See Sandbox.
Files served by Tess (filesystem store) carry nosniff and a sandboxing Content-Security-Policy. For S3 stores, keep the bucket private, and serve files through presigned URLs or a CDN.

Email uniqueness isn't enforced atomically. Two Admins creating the same email address at the same instant could both succeed. No built-in rate limiting beyond the per-account lockout. Put a rate limiter in front of /graphql (reverse proxy or API gateway). Single sign-on (OIDC) is planned for the Enterprise edition.

The Enterprise edition is for organizations using Tess commercially. It adds: Advanced features, built on top of the Community core. You can write and run your own plugins with either edition (see Plugins). Official Enterprise plugins are distributed as WebAssembly modules and installed exactly like your own.
Tess ships with an admin interface at /admin/. It's a static single-page app served by the Tess binary, and it talks to the same GraphQL API as your applications.

First run: when no account exists yet, the admin asks for the bootstrap token and the first Owner's details, then signs you in. Afterwards: sign in with your email and password. Tokens: API tokens and the bootstrap token can also be used, via Use an API/bootstrap token instead. Where the session lives: in the browser tab's session storage, never in local storage. Closing the tab signs you out.

Which pages you see depends on your role: Page Who What it does Content Everyone signed in The content manager: pick a content type, search and page through its entries (drafts included), and open one in a side panel. Every field type has its own control: text with length counter, Markdown (toolbar, image upload and a live preview side by side; raw HTML is flagged as you type), numbers, dates, UUID, password (write-only: leave empty to keep it), JSON, enums, relation pickers (with Upload… for Asset relations), components and dynamic zones (add, reorder, remove blocks). What you can do follows your role, see below. Content models Owner, Admin Create, edit and delete content types: API IDs, fields (every type with its options: length bounds and format presets for text, enum values, relation targets, components, dynamic zones…), descriptions, and the review workflow toggle. The built-in Asset type (media library) is read-only; reference it from your models with a relation field. Components Owner, Admin Create, edit and delete reusable groups of fields, and see which models use each one. See Components. Review queue Owner, Admin, Reviewer (and Contributors, read-only) Entries in review and with changes requested. A side panel compares the draft with the published version and shows the history; reviewers approve (optionally with a comment) or request changes (comment required). Users Owner, Admin Create, edit, disable and delete users; set roles and scope. Only Owners manage Owners, and there is always at least one Owner. API tokens Owner, Admin Create tokens with a role, scope and expiry (the secret is shown once), list and revoke them. Plugins Owner, Admin Upload WebAssembly modules, enable them, scope them to content types, configure them, allow outgoing hosts, read their last error. See Managing plugins. Search Owner, Admin Enable full-text search per model, pick the indexed fields (the engine schema of each one, generated from its type, is shown), and reindex. Needs TESS_SEARCH, see Search. My account Everyone signed in Change your password; sign out of every session.

The buttons shown mirror the server rules; the server has the last word. Role Create / edit drafts Publish, unpublish Submit for review Delete Owner, Admin Every type Every type Workflow types Any entry Contributor Types in their scope In scope, types without the review workflow In scope, workflow types In scope, entries never published Reviewer, Member — (read only) — — — Reviewers approve or request changes from the Review queue. API tokens signed in to the admin can edit only if they have an admin role.

Docker image: includes the admin under /admin/. Running from source: build it with cd admin && npm install && npm run build, then point TESS_ADMIN_DIR at admin/dist/client. Tess detects that folder automatically when started from the repository root. Development: npm run dev proxies /graphql, /api and /media to TESS_API_URL (default http://localhost:8080).

A content type (e.g. Post, Author, Page) is a model with typed fields: TEXT (with length bounds and an optional format), MARKDOWN, INT, FLOAT, BOOLEAN, DATETIME, DATE, UUID, PASSWORD (write-only), JSON, ENUM, RELATION to another type (one or many), COMPONENT and DYNAMIC_ZONE. Content types are created at runtime, and the GraphQL schema is rebuilt from them. See the GraphQL API. Components are reusable groups of fields (an SEO block, a hero banner) that you add to content types, nest in each other, or mix in dynamic zones to build pages from blocks. See Components. An entry is one item of a content type, such as a single blog post.

Every entry has a draft, which is what editors change, and optionally a published version, which is what the public reads. Publishing copies the draft to the published stage. Editing afterwards changes only the draft until the next publish. Queries take a stage argument (PUBLISHED by default).

Admins can enable a review workflow on any content type, typically pages and blog posts. On those types, contributors submit drafts for review, and reviewers approve them (which publishes them) or request changes with a comment: DRAFT ──submit──▶ IN_REVIEW ──approve──▶ PUBLISHED ▲ │ └─ CHANGES_REQUESTED ◀── request changes (with a comment) Editing an entry sets it back to DRAFT, so reviewers always approve exactly what gets published. Every step is recorded in the entry's history. See Workflow.

Owner Admin Contributor Reviewer Member Manage Owners ✔ Manage users, API tokens, content models, plugins ✔ ✔ Publish anything, bypass review ✔ ✔ Approve / request changes (workflow types) ✔ ✔ ✔ Create and edit drafts, submit for review, upload media ✔ ✔ ✔ Publish types without workflow ✔ ✔ ✔ Read drafts and media ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Scope: each Contributor or Reviewer can be limited to a list of content types, their scope. An empty scope means all. API tokens carry a role and a scope too. Anonymous requests can read published content, unless the operator disables public reads. Where the rules live: they are enforced in the core, so every surface (API, uploads, plugins) follows them. See Authentication.

The id of an entry is an opaque, encrypted token that expires (24 h by default). It changes on every response, and database ids are never exposed. Use the stable ref as a cache or list key, and route pages by your own fields, such as a slug. See Ids and refs.

Media: uploaded files are entries of the built-in Asset type. Any content type can reference them with a relation. See Media. Search: with Typesense configured, every content type with text fields gets a search<Plural> query. See Search. Plugins: sandboxed WebAssembly modules that validate, transform or react to changes. See Plugins.
Run Tess locally, create the first account, model some content and query it, in about five minutes.

cp .env.example .env # Fill in the four secrets, each with a different random value: # TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN, TESS_ID_SECRET, TESS_REF_SECRET, TESS_SESSION_SECRET openssl rand -hex 32 docker compose up --build To run every optional service too (S3 storage, search, cache and n8n workflows, all on your machine), use the local profile: scripts/init-env.sh --local then docker compose --profile local up --build. By default Tess stores content in an embedded RocksDB database and keeps uploaded files on disk, both in the tess-data volume. To use PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB, an S3 bucket or Typesense instead, see Docker.
scripts/dev-server.sh # in-memory database, random secrets, port 8080 The script writes its generated secrets to a private file (${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/tess-dev.env) and never prints them.

Until the first account exists, setupRequired is true. Open http://localhost:8080/admin/ and follow the Create the first Owner screen, which asks for the bootstrap token (TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN). You can also do it from a terminal: source "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/tess-dev.env" # or export TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN yourself curl -s http://localhost:8080/graphql \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H "authorization: Bearer $TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN" \ -d '{"query":"mutation { createUser(input: {email: \"ada@example.com\", name: \"Ada Example\", role: OWNER, password: \"choose a long passphrase\"}) { id role } }"}' warning The bootstrap token grants full access. Once the Owner exists, remove TESS_ADMIN_TOKEN from your configuration and restart.

mutation { login(email: "ada@example.com", password: "choose a long passphrase") { token expiresAt } } Send the returned token as Authorization: Bearer <token> with every request below. In the admin UI, just sign in with your email and password.

mutation { createContentType(input: { apiId: "Post" fields: [ { name: "title", type: TEXT, required: true } { name: "slug", type: TEXT } { name: "body", type: MARKDOWN } ] }) { apiId pluralApiId } } Tess immediately adds post, posts, createPost, updatePost, publishPost and friends to the schema.

mutation { createPost(data: { title: "Hello Tess", slug: "hello-tess", body: "First tile." }) { id } } mutation($id: ID!) { publishPost(id: $id) { stage title } } Anyone can now read it without a token, and the GraphiQL IDE at http://localhost:8080/graphql is a handy place to try: { posts(where: { slug: "hello-tess" }) { total items { ref title body publishedAt } } }
Concepts: stages, review workflow, roles, ids and refs. Admin UI: a tour of the admin. Build with the API: filters, auth, media, search. Deploy and operate: production setup.

Admins link calendars to Tess in Admin → Calendars, for reservations and events handled by n8n workflows: Calendar Role In n8n Google Calendar Receives events Tess → Calendar: create, update and cancel events; Google emails the invitations. List events. cal.diy booking page Sends bookings Tess Trigger on calendar.booking.created, …rescheduled, …cancelled; Tess → Calendar → Get Bookings. Credentials stay in Tess, encrypted with TESS_SECRETS_KEY. Workflows only use a Tess API token, so you can change accounts without touching them. Typical flows: Reservation form: a form form.submitted → Create Event in the "Reservations" Google calendar, with the visitor as attendee. Booking page: a guest books on cal.diy → calendar.booking.created → confirm on Slack, add the guest to your CRM, or mirror the booking into a Google calendar. Event content: an Event entry is published → Create Event with the date and place of the entry; entry.unpublish → Cancel Event.

In the Google Cloud console: Enable the Google Calendar API for your project. Configure the OAuth consent screen (internal for a Google Workspace domain; external otherwise, adding your accounts as test users until the app is published). Create an OAuth client ID of type Web application, with this authorized redirect URI (shown in Admin → Calendars): https://cms.example.com/api/calendars/google/callback Enter the client id and secret in Admin → Calendars → Google OAuth client (the secret is stored encrypted), or set TESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and TESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET on the server. Tess asks for the calendar scope (events and invitations) and the account's email address.

Link a Google calendar opens Google's sign-in. After consent, Google sends you back to the admin. Pick the calendar to link: any calendar the account can write to, including shared and group calendars. Link several calendars of the same account with Link a calendar next to it. Tess keeps the account's refresh token, encrypted, and refreshes access tokens by itself. Removing the account in Tess doesn't revoke Tess's access at Google: also remove it in the account's Google security settings.

From n8n, Tess → Calendar: Operation Fields Create Event Calendar, title, start, end, attendees, description, location, time zone, Send Invitations Update Event Event ID, and the fields to change Cancel Event Event ID; Send Invitations tells the attendees Get Events From, to (default: the next 30 days) Dates are RFC 3339 date-times (2026-12-24T19:00:00+01:00), local date-times with a time zone (2026-12-24T19:00:00 and Europe/Paris, the calendar's zone by default), or YYYY-MM-DD for all-day events. Attendees are emails, optionally with a name: Ada <ada@example.com>, grace@example.com. With Send Invitations, Google emails the invitation, the updates and the cancellation to the attendees, from the linked account. Each change emits calendar.event.created, …updated or …cancelled.

cal.diy is the MIT-licensed, self-hostable fork of Cal.com: visitors book a slot on its pages. Tess receives each booking change as a webhook, signed with a secret, and turns it into an event for your workflows. In Admin → Calendars → Link a cal.diy booking page, give a name and the public URL of the booking page. Tess shows a webhook URL and a secret (shown once). In cal.diy, Settings → Developer → Webhooks → New: paste the URL and the secret, and choose the triggers (booking created, rescheduled, cancelled…). Each booking then emits an event, with the booking normalized and the original cal.diy payload in raw: { "event": "calendar.booking.created", "data": { "calendar": { "id": "…", "name": "Table booking", "provider": "CALDIY" }, "booking": { "trigger": "BOOKING_CREATED", "uid": "…", "title": "Table for 2", "start": "2026-12-24T18:00:00Z", "end": "2026-12-24T20:00:00Z", "attendees": [{ "email": "ada@example.com", "name": "Ada", "timeZone": "Europe/Paris" }], "organizer": { "email": "chef@example.com", "name": "Chef" } }, "raw": { "triggerEvent": "BOOKING_CREATED", "payload": { "…": "…" } } } } cal.diy trigger Tess event BOOKING_CREATED calendar.booking.created BOOKING_RESCHEDULED calendar.booking.rescheduled (rescheduleUid is the replaced booking) BOOKING_CANCELLED calendar.booking.cancelled BOOKING_REQUESTED, BOOKING_REJECTED calendar.booking.requested, …rejected Any other calendar.booking.updated Requests without a valid x-cal-signature-256 get a 403. New secret replaces it, and the webhook in cal.diy must be updated. The last 100 bookings are listed in Admin → Calendars → Bookings. Tess doesn't create cal.diy bookings: visitors book on cal.diy's pages.

The caldiy profile runs cal.diy next to Tess, on the same PostgreSQL server, so you operate a single database server. cal.diy gets its own caldiy database and role, created by the caldiy-db-init service, and Tess uses the tess database: scripts/init-env.sh --calendar caldiy # Tess on PostgreSQL + cal.diy secrets docker compose --profile caldiy up -d # starts postgres, caldiy-db-init, caldiy and tess Setting TESS_DATABASE=postgres, DATABASE_URL, POSTGRES_PASSWORD Tess on the shared server (init-env.sh --calendar caldiy sets them). CALDIY_PUBLIC_URL Where browsers reach cal.diy (default http://localhost:3001). CALDIY_DB_PASSWORD Password of cal.diy's caldiy database role. CALDIY_NEXTAUTH_SECRET, CALDIY_ENCRYPTION_KEY cal.diy's own secrets. CALDIY_SMTP_*, CALDIY_EMAIL_FROM Optional: booking confirmation emails. CALDIY_GOOGLE_API_CREDENTIALS Optional: Google Calendar inside cal.diy (availability). cal.diy publishes no Docker image yet, so Compose builds it from source on first start. Pin the source with CALDIY_REF, a commit of the cal.diy repository. The build takes several minutes and about 6 GB of memory; later starts reuse the image. Open cal.diy at CALDIY_PUBLIC_URL and create its admin account. In the same Compose project, cal.diy reaches Tess at http://tess:8080: use http://tess:8080/api/calendars/<id>/webhook as the subscriber URL. cal.diy's own documentation recommends it for personal, non-production use.

Owner / Admin Contributor Reviewer, Member Link and unlink calendars, Google client ✔ Create, update, cancel events ✔ ✔ with the calendar scope Read events and bookings ✔ ✔ with the calendar scope ✔ with the calendar scope An empty scope gives access to everything, calendar included. For an n8n workflow, an API token with the Contributor role and the scope calendar is enough.

query { calendars { id name provider enabled timeZone bookingUrl } } mutation($c: ID!) { createCalendarEvent(calendarId: $c, sendInvitations: true, input: { title: "Dinner for 4", start: "2026-12-24T19:00:00", end: "2026-12-24T21:00:00", timeZone: "Europe/Paris", attendees: [{ email: "ada@example.com", name: "Ada" }] }) { id link attendees { email status } } } query($c: ID!) { calendarEvents(calendarId: $c, from: "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z", to: "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z") { id title start end } } query($c: ID!) { calendarBookings(calendarId: $c) { event uid title start attendees { email } } }
Variable Default TESS_CALENDARS true false turns calendars off. TESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, TESS_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET unset Google OAuth client; replaces the one set in the admin.

Tess collects the forms of your websites and apps (contact, reservation, sign-up, survey…) without a form service. Admins define each form in Admin → Forms. Your front-end renders it from its public definition and posts the answers to Tess. Tess validates and keeps them, and sends a form.submitted event to your webhooks, so an n8n workflow can act on every submission. Forms are headless: Tess serves no HTML. Your front-end controls the design.

In Admin → Forms → New form: Title and slug: the slug is in the URL, /api/forms/<slug>. Fields, in order. Each has a label, a name (the key of the value in submissions, e.g. email), a type, and whether it is required: Type Value Checked Text, Long text text length (1,000 / 10,000 characters by default) Email, Phone, URL text format (URL: http(s)://…) Number number min / max Date YYYY-MM-DD a valid date Date and time YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM a valid date and time Choice one of the options Multiple choice a list of options Checkbox true / false a required checkbox must be checked (e.g. "I accept the terms") Success message, returned to your front-end after a submission. Redirect URL, for plain HTML forms (see below). Accept submissions: a closed form answers 404 and its definition is hidden.

The definition is public: curl https://cms.example.com/api/forms/contact { "slug": "contact", "title": "Contact us", "fields": [ { "name": "email", "label": "Email", "type": "EMAIL", "required": true }, { "name": "topic", "label": "Topic", "type": "SELECT", "required": false, "options": ["Sales", "Support"] }, { "name": "message", "label": "Message", "type": "TEXTAREA", "required": true } ], "successMessage": "Thanks, we'll get back to you soon.", "honeypot": "_hp" } Post the answers as JSON: const res = await fetch("https://cms.example.com/api/forms/contact", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ email: "ada@example.com", topic: "Sales", message: "Hello!" }), }); const body = await res.json(); // 201: { ok: true, id, message } · 400: { error, fields: { email: "must be an email address" } } Answer Meaning 201 Stored; message is the success message. 400 Invalid: fields has an error message per field, to show next to it. 404 No open form with this slug. 413 The body is over 64 KiB. 429 The visitor posted too often (see the rate limit below); retry after Retry-After seconds. Unknown keys are ignored, and values are normalized: trimmed text, numbers as numbers, checkboxes as booleans.
documents.s: Using a form in a front-end

documents.t: No JavaScript needed: post the form directly. Repeated names (multiple choice) become a list. With a redirect URL, the browser is sent there after a successful submission. Otherwise it gets the JSON answer. <form method="post" action="https://cms.example.com/api/forms/contact"> <input name="email" type="email" required> <select name="topic"><option>Sales</option><option>Support</option></select> <textarea name="message" required></textarea> <!-- Anti-spam: keep it hidden and empty. --> <input name="_hp" hidden tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off"> <button>Send</button> </form> Calls from a browser on another origin need that origin in TESS_CORS_ORIGINS (the default * allows all).

Honeypot: add a hidden field named _hp and keep it empty. Bots fill it; Tess then answers as usual but drops the submission. Rate limit: each visitor (IP address) can post TESS_FORMS_RATE_LIMIT submissions per form per minute (default 10). Behind a reverse proxy, Tess reads the visitor's address from X-Forwarded-For when the connection comes from a private or local address.

Admin → Forms → Submissions lists them, newest first, with the page they were posted from. Select some to delete them, or Export CSV. Submissions contain personal data: export and delete them according to your privacy policy. Deleting a form deletes its submissions. They are stored in the settings store of your database, so forms work with every backend.

Every stored submission emits form.submitted: { "event": "form.submitted", "data": { "form": { "id": "…", "slug": "contact", "title": "Contact us" }, "submission": { "id": "…", "formId": "…", "data": { "email": "ada@example.com", "message": "Hello!" }, "submittedAt": "…", "source": "https://www.example.com/contact" } } } In n8n, start a workflow with the Tess Trigger on form.submitted, then use {{ $json.data.submission.data.email }}. For example: a reservation form → Tess → Calendar → Create Event in a linked Google calendar, with the visitor as attendee, so Google emails the invitation (see Calendars); a contact form → send an email or a Slack message, or create a ticket; a sign-up form → add the person to your newsletter tool. The Tess node also reads submissions (Form → Get Submissions).

mutation { createForm(input: { slug: "contact", title: "Contact us", successMessage: "Thanks!", fields: [ { name: "email", label: "Email", type: EMAIL, required: true } { name: "message", label: "Message", type: TEXTAREA, required: true } ] }) { id } } query { forms { id slug title enabled submissionCount } } query($id: ID!) { formSubmissions(formId: $id, first: 50) { total items { data submittedAt source } } } mutation($id: ID!, $ids: [ID!]!) { deleteFormSubmissions(formId: $id, ids: $ids) } updateForm replaces the definition and keeps the submissions. Renaming a field leaves the values already submitted under the old name.
Variable Default TESS_FORMS true false turns forms off. TESS_FORMS_RATE_LIMIT 10 Submissions per visitor and form, per minute.

n8n automates Tess: start workflows on Tess events, read and write content and translations, and connect hundreds of other services (Slack, email, AI translation, CI…). Tess embeds the n8n editor in the admin UI (Workflows, for Admins and Contributors), served by Tess under /n8n/ so it shares the admin's origin. browser ──▶ Tess /admin/workflows ── iframe ──▶ Tess /n8n/* ──(proxy)──▶ n8n n8n ── Tess node (GraphQL, API token) ──────────────────────────────▶ Tess /graphql Tess ── webhook (signed events) ──▶ Tess Trigger node in n8n :::caution License n8n is distributed under the Sustainable Use License: running it for your own internal workflows is fine, but offering it embedded in a product to third parties requires a commercial n8n Embed license from n8n. For this reason, Tess's commercial license (TESS_LICENSE=commercial) does not include the embedded editor: Tess doesn't proxy /n8n/, and Workflows disappears from the admin. Webhooks still send every event, to n8n or any other tool you run under your own license. :::

Tess Trigger starts the workflow on the selected events (entry.publish, entry.*, contentType.update, i18n.translation.update…), optionally for some content types. Activating the workflow registers a webhook in Tess (listed under Admin → Webhooks, managed by n8n); deactivating removes it. Signatures are verified. If Tess reaches n8n at another address than the public one, set n8n URL for Tess (e.g. http://n8n:5678). Tess reads and writes through the GraphQL API: Resource Operations Entry Get, Get Many (filter, stage, limit), Create, Update, Delete, Publish, Unpublish Translation Get Keys (search, missing in a language), Set Text (text and/or review state), Export, Publish to delivery targets Calendar Create Event (with invitations), Update Event, Cancel Event, Get Events, Get Bookings (calendars) Form Get Submissions (forms) GraphQL Any query or mutation, with variables After a Tess Trigger, {{ $json.data.entry.id }} and {{ $json.contentType }} point at the changed entry.

entry.publish → rebuild a static site (GitHub repository_dispatch, Netlify, Vercel hook). i18n.key.create → machine-translate the new key, save it as TRANSLATED for review. entry.submit → notify reviewers on Slack or by email. contentType.update → regenerate client types in a repository. form.submitted (a reservation form) → create the event in a Google calendar with Tess → Calendar → Create Event, which emails the invitation. calendar.booking.created (cal.diy) → add the guest to a mailing list, or post the booking on Slack.

The editor's live updates use server-sent events, which the Tess proxy streams; WebSockets are not proxied (hence N8N_PUSH_BACKEND=sse). Responses written by workflows (/n8n/webhook/*, /n8n/form/*) are sandboxed with a Content-Security-Policy so they cannot run scripts with the Tess admin's origin. The proxy is not available on AWS Lambda, nor behind the Passenger launcher (it buffers responses): link to n8n on its own domain there.

Tess manages the translations of your apps and sites, in the spirit of Tolgee: translation keys, languages, a review step, import/export in the usual file formats, live files over HTTP and delivery to object storage (Garage, AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO, Azure Blob). Everything is in the admin UI under Translations, and in the GraphQL API.

Language A BCP 47 tag (en, fr-CA, zh-Hant). One of them is the base language translators start from. Key A message, e.g. home.title, in an optional namespace (common, checkout; empty = default), with a description for translators, tags and a plural flag. Translation The text of a key in a language, written in ICU MessageFormat: Hello {name}, {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}. State TRANSLATED (to review) or REVIEWED. A missing translation is untranslated. Changing a text sends it back to TRANSLATED. Translations are stored in the settings store of your database backend, so they work with every backend (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB, DynamoDB, RocksDB).

Tess serves the current translations at /i18n/{format}/{file}, with the same layout as an export: curl https://cms.example.com/i18n/json-nested/fr.json curl https://cms.example.com/i18n/i18next/fr/common.json Format names in URLs: json, json-nested, i18next, arb, xliff, po, properties, android, apple, yaml, csv. In Translations → Serving, Admins choose whether the files are public (also requires TESS_PUBLIC_READ), whether only reviewed texts are served, and whether missing texts fall back to the base language. For production traffic, publish to a delivery target behind a CDN instead.

Admins register webhooks (admin UI → Webhooks, or the GraphQL API): Tess then POSTs a signed JSON event to each subscribed URL when content, models or translations change. The n8n integration registers its webhooks by itself.

PASSWORD fields are never sent. Opaque ids expire (TESS_ID_TTL): use them soon, or match entries by ref.

Each request has the headers X-Tess-Event, X-Tess-Delivery, X-Tess-Webhook and X-Tess-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<t>.<raw body>")> The signing secret is shown once when the webhook is created (and by Rotate secret). Reject requests whose signature does not match or whose t is too old: import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto"; function verify(secret, header, rawBody, toleranceSeconds = 300) { const { t, v1 } = Object.fromEntries(header.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=", 2))); if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(t)) > toleranceSeconds) return false; const expected = createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${t}.`).update(rawBody).digest(); const given = Buffer.from(v1 ?? "", "hex"); return given.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(given, expected); } Extra headers (e.g. an API key the receiver expects) can be added; their values are encrypted at rest and write-only.

Deliveries run in the background. Network errors, 408, 429 and 5xx are retried up to TESS_WEBHOOK_MAX_ATTEMPTS times (after 10 s, 1 min, 5 min, 30 min). Other 4xx answers are final. Redirects are not followed. Pending retries live in memory: a restart drops them. On AWS Lambda, deliveries happen within the request, with one attempt. The last 25 deliveries of each webhook (status, HTTP code, error, attempts, duration) are shown under Deliveries and by webhookDeliveries. TESS_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS restricts the hosts webhooks may target.

Tess (from tessera, a single tile of a mosaic) is a self-hostable, GraphQL-first headless CMS written in Rust, in the spirit of Strapi and Hygraph. Every content entry is a tile; your websites, apps and services are the mosaic.

Content models defined at runtime. Create content types in the admin UI or through the API, and Tess regenerates its GraphQL schema on the fly: queries, filters, sorting, pagination, relations and mutations. Draft and publish on every entry, plus an optional review workflow per content type: submit, then approve or request changes. Users and roles: Owner, Admin, Contributor, Reviewer and Member, each user optionally limited to some content types. API tokens cover CI and front-end builds. Any database. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite (one SeaQuery-based backend), MongoDB, DynamoDB, embedded RocksDB, or in-memory. All of them pass the same conformance suite, so they behave identically. Media library on S3-compatible storage (Garage, MinIO, AWS S3, R2…) or the local filesystem, with direct presigned uploads. Full-text search with Typesense. Plugins: sandboxed WebAssembly modules that admins upload and configure at runtime. You can write them in Rust, Go, JavaScript and more. Opaque, expiring, encrypted ids in the API; database ids never leave the server. One binary, two runtimes: an HTTP server for Docker, VMs or Kubernetes, or an AWS Lambda function. The runtime is detected automatically.

Hygraph and Tess are both GraphQL-first, so the move is mostly mechanical: Describe your models and components in a Tess models file. Import the models with tess-transfer. Copy assets and entries with a GraphQL-to-GraphQL script. Adapt your front-end queries: most of them only change shape slightly. Hygraph is only read, so you can rehearse the migration as often as you like. Start with a fresh Tess instance (see Quick start) and an Admin token for it.

Hygraph Tess Notes Single line text, Slug TEXT Slugs with a pattern such as ^[a-z0-9-]+$. Tess caps TEXT at 80 characters unless you set maxLength. Multi line text TEXT maxLength: null (unlimited). Markdown MARKDOWN Tess rejects raw HTML in Markdown. Rich Text MARKDOWN Query { markdown } and convert (see the script). Or keep { json } in a JSON field. Int, Float, Boolean INT, FLOAT, BOOLEAN Date, DateTime DATE, DATETIME JSON JSON Enumeration ENUM Same value rules (GraphQL names). Color TEXT Query { hex }. Location COMPONENT A Location component with latitude and longitude (FLOAT). Asset RELATION to Asset many: true for multiple assets. Reference RELATION many: true for multiple references. A reference to several models (union) becomes one relation field per model. Basic component COMPONENT repeatable: true for "allow multiple values". Modular component DYNAMIC_ZONE The allowed components. "Allow multiple values" on a scalar JSON Stores the list. Also: Stages: PUBLISHED and DRAFT work the same way in Tess (and the stage argument has the same name). Custom stages, such as QA, aren't copied. Localization: Tess has no per-entry locales yet. Copy one locale per run (add locales: [fr] to the Hygraph queries), into one model per language or a model with a locale ENUM field. For UI strings, use Translations. Remote sources and remote fields are not content: keep calling those services from your front-end, or from a plugin. System fields (id, createdAt, publishedAt, createdBy…) are set by Tess.

In Hygraph, create a Permanent Auth Token (Project settings → Access → Permanent Auth Tokens) with read access to the DRAFT and PUBLISHED stages, and copy the Content API endpoint. Then edit the MODELS list at the top of the script: one line per model, the fields to copy as a GraphQL selection, the relations, the conversions and the renamed fields. export HYGRAPH_URL=https://<region>.cdn.hygraph.com/content/<project>/master HYGRAPH_TOKEN=… export TESS_URL=https://cms.example.com TESS_TOKEN=… node hygraph.mjs The script needs Node.js 20 or later and has no dependencies. It: Uploads every asset to Tess, with its dimensions, and publishes it. Creates the entries without their relations: published documents as published (the version visitors see), draft-only documents as drafts. Modular component items (__typename) become dynamic zone items. Links references and assets in a second pass, then republishes. Lists published documents with unpublished changes in Hygraph, so editors can redo those edits in Tess. hygraph.mjs #!/usr/bin/env node // Copyright © 2026 Tess Dev Team <https://tessheadless.com> // SPDX-License-Identifier: LicenseRef-Tess-Community-Enterprise // Community edition: personal use. null }, // Relations, filled in a second pass: field → `assets` or a model's `query`. relations: { coverImage: "assets", category: "categories", authors: "authors" }, // Hygraph field → Tess field, when they differ. rename: { content: "body" }, }, { query: "authors", tess: "Author", select: "name bio" }, ]; const env = (name) => process.env[name]?.replace(/\/$/, "") || fail(`set ${name}`); const HYGRAPH = env("HYGRAPH_URL"); const HYGRAPH_TOKEN = env("HYGRAPH_TOKEN"); const TESS = env("TESS_URL"); const TESS_TOKEN = env("TESS_TOKEN"); function fail(message) { console.error(message); process.exit(1); } async function graphql(url, token, query, variables = {}) { const res = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ query, variables }), }); const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({ errors: [{ message: `HTTP ${res.status}` }] })); if (body.errors?.length) throw new Error(`${url}: ${body.errors.map((e) => e.message).join("; ")}`); return body.data; } const hygraph = (q, v) => graphql(HYGRAPH, HYGRAPH_TOKEN, q, v); const tess = (q, v) => graphql(`${TESS}/graphql`, TESS_TOKEN, q, v); /** Every document of a model in one stage (`DRAFT` holds the latest version of all). */ async function all(query, selection, stage) { const items = []; for (let skip = 0; ; skip += 100) { const data = await hygraph( `query($skip: Int!, $stage: Stage!) { items: ${query}(first: 100, skip: $skip, stage: $stage) { ${selection} } }`, { skip, stage }, ); items.push(...data.items); if (data.items.length < 100) return items; } } // ---- 1. Assets: Hygraph id → Tess asset id ----------------------------------- const assets = new Map(); for (const a of await all("assets", "id url fileName mimeType width height", "DRAFT")) { const bytes = await (await fetch(a.url)).arrayBuffer(); const res = await fetch(`${TESS}/media/upload?fileName=${encodeURIComponent(a.fileName)}`, { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${TESS_TOKEN}`, "Content-Type": a.mimeType ??
